title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Overview
Learning Objectives:

Understand what hierarchical models are and why they’re useful
Learn when to use hierarchical models vs. standard regression
Master the concepts of pooling: complete, none, and partial
Apply hierarchical models using rstanarm and brms in R
Interpret Bayesian results appropriately for environmental data
Make informed decisions about model structure

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Why Hierarchical Models?
Environmental data naturally has structure
— sites within regions, measurements over time, species within ecosystems. Hierarchical models respect this structure.

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
What are Hierarchical Models?
Definition: Statistical models that account for data collected at multiple levels or with nested structure.
Also Known As:

Mixed-effects models
Multilevel models
Random effects models
Nested models

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Key Idea
Some observations are more similar to each other than to others because they share common features (same site, same species, same year).
Example in Environmental Science:

Water quality measurements from multiple lakes
Each lake has multiple sampling sites
Each site measured multiple times
Measurements within a lake are more similar than across lakes

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
The Problem: Clustered Data
Real-World Scenario:
You’re studying mercury contamination in fish across 20 lakes. You catch 10 fish per lake and measure mercury levels and length of each fish. You want to build a model that relates fish length to mercury concentration.
Question: How should we analyze these 200 measurements?
The Issue:

Fish from the same lake are more similar than fish from different lakes
They share the same water chemistry, food web, temperature
Standard regression assumes all observations are independent
Ignoring lake structure leads to incorrect conclusions

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Consequences of Ignoring Structure

Underestimated standard errors → inflated Type I error rates
False confidence in results
Poor predictions for new lakes
Missing important sources of variation

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
The Pooling Problem
Three Approaches to Handling Groups:


1. Complete Pooling (Ignore Groups)

Treat all fish as if they came from one giant lake
Simple but wrong
Ignores important variation between lakes


2. No Pooling (Separate Models)

Fit completely separate model for each lake
20 independent analyses
Loses information, can’t compare lakes
Terrible for lakes with few fish


3. Partial Pooling (Hierarchical Model)

Model each lake separately BUT
Share information across lakes
Best of both worlds!


Let’s explore each approach…

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Complete Pooling: Ignore the Structure
The Model:
\[
\text{mercury}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{length}_i + \epsilon_i
\] where i indexes fish.


What This Means:

One grand mean (\(\beta_0\)) for all lakes
Same relationship (\(\beta_1\)) everywhere
Assumes all lakes are identical

When It Might Be OK:

Groups are truly irrelevant to the question
Interest is only in population average
Rarely appropriate for environmental data


Problems:

Clearly wrong—lakes differ in baseline mercury
Pretends we have 200 independent fish
Standard errors too small (overconfident)
Can’t make lake-specific predictions

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
No Pooling: Treat Groups Independently
The Model:
\[
\text{mercury}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_1 \times \text{length}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}
\] where j indexes lake and i indexes fish within lake j. This is equivalent to fitting 20 separate regressions


What This Means:

Each lake gets its own intercept (β₀j)
20 separate analyses
No information shared between lakes

When It Might Be OK:

Groups are fundamentally different
Abundant data in each group
No interest in new groups
Sometimes reasonable but wasteful


Problems:

Estimates for small lakes are very uncertain
Can’t make predictions for new lakes
Ignores fact that lakes come from common distribution
Extreme estimates for unusual lakes

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Partial Pooling: The Hierarchical Solution
The Model:
Level 1 (fish): \(\text{mercury}_{ij} = \alpha_j + \beta × \text{length}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}\)
Level 2 (lake): \(\alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_\alpha, \sigma_\alpha)\)
where j indexes lake and i indexes fish within lake j.


What This Means:

Each lake has its own intercept (\(\alpha_j\))
BUT lake intercepts come from a common distribution
Lakes with little data “borrow strength” from others
Information sharing!


Why This Works:

Respects that lakes differ (random intercepts)
Recognizes lakes are samples from population
Automatically balances group vs. population information
Produces “shrinkage” toward population mean


This is What Makes Hierarchical Models Powerful!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
section: Shrinkage: The Magic of Partial Pooling
text:
Shrinkage: The Magic of Partial Pooling
What is Shrinkage?
Estimates for individual groups are pulled toward the overall mean, with the amount of pull depending on:

How much data in that group
How variable the group is
How different it is from other groups

The Formula (Conceptually):
group_estimate = w × group_data + (1-w) × population_mean
where w depends on sample size and variability

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Practical Example

Lake with 2 fish: mostly uses population info (w ≈ 0.2)
Lake with 50 fish: mostly uses own data (w ≈ 0.9)



Code
library(rstanarm)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Create simulated lake mercury data with varying sample sizes
# This reflects the "8 lakes with different sample sizes" concept
lake_info <- data.frame(
  lake = paste0("Lake_", LETTERS[1:8]),
  sample_size = c(50, 30, 20, 15, 10, 5, 3, 2), # Varying sample sizes
  true_intercept = c(2.0, 2.8, 1.5, 3.2, 1.8, 2.5, 1.2, 3.5) # True lake effects
)

# Generate fish data
fish_data <- map_dfr(1:nrow(lake_info), function(i) {
  lake <- lake_info$lake[i]
  n <- lake_info$sample_size[i]
  true_int <- lake_info$true_intercept[i]

  data.frame(
    lake = lake,
    fish_id = 1:n,
    length = rnorm(n, mean = 25, sd = 5), # Fish length (cm)
    mercury = rnorm(n, mean = true_int + 0.05 * rnorm(n, 25, 5), sd = 0.3)
  )
})

# 1. COMPLETE POOLING (ignore lake structure)
complete_pool <- stan_glm(
  mercury ~ length,
  data = fish_data,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 1000,
  refresh = 0, # Suppress output
  seed = 123
)

# 2. NO POOLING (separate models for each lake)
no_pool_estimates <- fish_data %>%
  group_by(lake) %>%
  summarise(
    intercept = mean(mercury - 0.05 * length), # Crude estimate
    n_fish = n(),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# 3. PARTIAL POOLING (hierarchical model)
partial_pool <- stan_glmer(
  mercury ~ length + (1 | lake),
  data = fish_data,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 1000,
  refresh = 0,
  seed = 123
)

# Extract estimates for comparison
complete_pool_int <- fixef(complete_pool)[1]
partial_pool_ints <- coef(partial_pool)$lake[, 1]
population_mean <- fixef(partial_pool)[1]

# Create comparison data frame
comparison_data <- data.frame(
  lake = lake_info$lake,
  sample_size = lake_info$sample_size,
  true_intercept = lake_info$true_intercept,
  complete_pooling = complete_pool_int,
  no_pooling = no_pool_estimates$intercept,
  partial_pooling = partial_pool_ints,
  population_mean = population_mean
)

# Calculate shrinkage factor (w) - how much each lake relies on its own data
comparison_data <- comparison_data %>%
  mutate(
    shrinkage_factor = abs(no_pooling - population_mean) /
      abs(partial_pooling - population_mean),
    w_approx = pmin(0.9, pmax(0.1, sample_size / (sample_size + 10))) # Approximate weight
  )

# Reshape for plotting
plot_data <- comparison_data %>%
  select(
    lake,
    sample_size,
    true_intercept,
    complete_pooling,
    no_pooling,
    partial_pooling
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(complete_pooling, no_pooling, partial_pooling),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    method = factor(
      method,
      levels = c("complete_pooling", "no_pooling", "partial_pooling"),
      labels = c("Complete Pooling", "No Pooling", "Partial Pooling")
    )
  )

# Create the visualization showing different pooling strategies
p1 <- ggplot(
  plot_data,
  aes(
    x = reorder(lake, sample_size),
    y = estimate,
    color = method,
    shape = method
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = population_mean,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = true_intercept), color = "black", shape = 4, size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "darkgreen")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15)) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Pooling Strategies",
    subtitle = "Black X = True value, Dashed line = Population mean",
    x = "Lake (ordered by sample size)",
    y = "Estimated Mercury Intercept (μg/g)",
    color = "Method",
    shape = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# Add sample sizes to x-axis labels
plot_data_labeled <- plot_data %>%
  left_join(
    comparison_data %>% select(lake, sample_size),
    by = c("lake", "sample_size")
  ) %>%
  mutate(lake_label = paste0(lake, "\n(n=", sample_size, ")"))

p1_labeled <- ggplot(
  plot_data_labeled,
  aes(
    x = reorder(lake_label, sample_size),
    y = estimate,
    color = method,
    shape = method
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = population_mean,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = true_intercept), color = "black", shape = 4, size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "darkgreen")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15)) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Pooling Strategies by Sample Size",
    subtitle = "Black X = True value, Dashed line = Population mean\nNote how partial pooling shrinks small-sample estimates toward the mean",
    x = "Lake (sample size)",
    y = "Estimated Mercury Intercept (μg/g)",
    color = "Method",
    shape = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))

# Show shrinkage effect more clearly
p2 <- comparison_data %>%
  select(lake, sample_size, no_pooling, partial_pooling, population_mean) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_size)) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(xend = sample_size, y = no_pooling, yend = partial_pooling),
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 1.5,
    color = "purple"
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(y = no_pooling), color = "blue", size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = partial_pooling),
    color = "darkgreen",
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = population_mean,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(y = partial_pooling, label = lake), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Shrinkage Effect in Partial Pooling",
    subtitle = "Blue = No pooling, Green = Partial pooling\nLines show how estimates are 'shrunk' toward population mean",
    x = "Sample Size (number of fish)",
    y = "Estimated Mercury Intercept (μg/g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Print the plots
print(p1_labeled)









Code
print(p2)









Code
# Show the shrinkage weights
cat("\nShrinkage Analysis:\n")
cat("Lakes with small samples get 'shrunk' more toward population mean:\n\n")
comparison_data %>%
  arrange(sample_size) %>%
  select(lake, sample_size, w_approx) %>%
  mutate(
    w_approx = round(w_approx, 2),
    interpretation = case_when(
      w_approx < 0.3 ~ "Mostly uses population info",
      w_approx < 0.7 ~ "Balanced combination",
      TRUE ~ "Mostly uses own data"
    )
  ) %>%
  print()

# Model comparison
cat("\nModel Summary:\n")
cat("Partial Pooling Model (Hierarchical):\n")
print(partial_pool)

# Extract and show ICC
icc_value <- VarCorr(partial_pool)$lake[1, 1] /
  (VarCorr(partial_pool)$lake[1, 1] + sigma(partial_pool)^2)
cat(sprintf("\nIntraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC): %.3f\n", icc_value))
cat("This means", round(icc_value * 100, 1), "% of variance is between lakes\n")


Complete Pooling:

All fish: one line
Ignores lakes entirely

No Pooling:

8 completely separate lines
Wild variation for small-sample lakes
Lake C (n=3): crazy extreme estimate

Partial Pooling:

8 different lines
Small-sample lakes pulled toward average
Lake C’s estimate is moderated
Uncertainty properly reflects sample size

The Pattern:

Large-sample lakes: similar in no-pooling vs partial-pooling
Small-sample lakes: shrunk toward population mean
This is automatic and optimal!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
When to Use Hierarchical Models
You Should Use Hierarchical Models When:
✓ Nested/Grouped Structure

Multiple sites within regions
Repeated measurements on same individuals/locations
Multiple species, plots, watersheds

✓ Interest in Group-Level Variation

How much do lakes differ in baseline mercury?
What’s the variance between sites?
Are groups meaningfully different?

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
When to Use Hierarchical Models
You Should Use Hierarchical Models When:
✓ Predictions for New Groups

Predict mercury for an unsampled lake
Estimate values for new sites
Generalize beyond observed groups

✓ Unbalanced Data

Some groups have many observations, others few
Hierarchical models handle this gracefully
No need to throw away data!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
When to Use Hierarchical Models (Examples)
Environmental Science Examples:
1. Spatial Hierarchical Structure

Problem: Measuring nitrogen runoff from 50 farms across 5 watersheds
Why Hierarchical: Farms within a watershed share hydrology, soil, climate
Model: Farm-level measurements nested in watersheds

2. Temporal Hierarchical Structure

Problem: Species counts at 20 sites over 10 years
Why Hierarchical: Repeated measures at same sites aren’t independent
Model: Yearly observations nested within sites

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
When to Use Hierarchical Models (Examples)
Environmental Science Examples:
3. Taxonomic Hierarchical Structure

Problem: Testing pollutant effects on 30 fish species from 4 families
Why Hierarchical: Species within family share biology
Model: Species nested within families

4. Multi-Level Spatial

Problem: Tree growth in plots within forests within ecoregions
Why Hierarchical: Three levels of grouping!
Model: Plots within forests within regions

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
section: Problem: Which Model for Bird Surveys?
text:
Problem: Which Model for Bird Surveys?
Scenario:
You conduct bird surveys at 30 sites across a mountain gradient. Each site is visited 4 times during breeding season.
Data Structure:

30 sites × 4 visits = 120 observations
Want to relate bird abundance to elevation

Question: What model should you use?
A. Standard Linear Model (ignore sites)
abundance ~ elevation
B. Fixed Effects for Sites
abundance ~ elevation + site
C. Hierarchical Model
Level 1: abundance_ij ~ elevation_j + α_j
Level 2: α_j ~ Normal(μ, σ)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Answer: C! Why?

Visits within sites are not independent (repeated measures)
Want to generalize to other sites on mountain
Sites are random sample from population of possible sites
Interested in site-to-site variation

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Bayesian Approach to Hierarchical Models
Why Bayesian for Hierarchical Models?

Natural Framework

Hierarchical structure maps directly to Bayesian model
Hyperparameters get hyperpriors—it’s all just probability!

Handles Complexity

Complex models fit without approximations
Correctly propagates uncertainty through levels

Small Sample Sizes

Works well even with few groups or observations per group
No asymptotic assumptions needed

Interpretable Uncertainty

Full posterior distributions for everything
Credible intervals have direct interpretation
Uncertainty about variance components

Predictive Distributions

Easy to predict for new groups
Accounts for all sources of uncertainty

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Bayesian Building Blocks
Quick Bayesian Refresher:
Bayes’ Theorem:
Posterior ∝ Likelihood × Prior
P(θ|data) ∝ P(data|θ) × P(θ)
Components:

Likelihood: P(data|θ) = How likely are the data given parameters?
Prior: P(θ) = What do we believe before seeing data?
Posterior: P(θ|data) = Updated beliefs after seeing data

In Hierarchical Models:

Parameters at each level get distributions
Hyperparameters control group-level distributions
Everything estimated simultaneously

Practical Interpretation:

95% Credible Interval: “Given the data, there’s a 95% probability the parameter is in this range”
Direct probability statements!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Hierarchical Model Structure
General Form:
Level 1 (Observation Level):
\[
y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma_{y}) \\
\mu_{ij} = \alpha_j + \beta \times x_{ij}
\]
Level 2 (Group Level):
\[
\alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{\alpha}, \sigma_{\alpha})
\]
Level 3 (Population Level / Priors):
\[
\mu_{\alpha} \sim \text{Normal}(0, 10) \\
\sigma_{\alpha} \sim \text{Cauchy}(0, 2.5) \\
\beta \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5) \\
\sigma_{y} \sim \text{Cauchy}(0, 2.5)
\]

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
What This Means:

Observations vary within groups (\(\sigma_y\))
Groups vary within population (\(\sigma_{\alpha}\))
Both sources of variation estimated
Priors express prior knowledge (often weakly informative)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Fixed vs Random Effects
Terminology (Often Confusing!):
Fixed Effects:

Parameters we estimate and care about
Examples: slope of elevation, effect of temperature
Same across all groups (though can vary in mixed models)

Random Effects:

Parameters that vary by group
Assume groups drawn from population distribution
Examples: lake-specific intercepts, site-level variation
Focus is on the distribution (mean and variance), not individual values

Helpful Distinction:

Fixed: “These specific effects”
Random: “Variation among similar things”

In Environmental Models:

Fixed: covariate effects (temperature, elevation, treatment)
Random: site effects, year effects, species effects
Both can be in the same model!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Introduction to rstanarm
What is rstanarm?
An R package that fits Bayesian regression models using Stan, with syntax similar to base R.
Key Features:

Familiar formula syntax (lm, lmer style)
Pre-compiled models (fast!)
Sensible default priors
Easy to use, hard to misuse

Installation:
install.packages("rstanarm")
library(rstanarm)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Basic Syntax:
# Standard regression
model <- stan_glm(y ~ x, data = mydata)

# Hierarchical model (like lme4)
model <- stan_glmer(y ~ x + (1 | group), data = mydata)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Advantages for Beginners:

Simple syntax
Good defaults
Extensive documentation
Active community

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Introduction to brms
What is brms?
Bayesian Regression Models using Stan
— more flexible than rstanarm.
Key Features:

Extremely flexible model specification
Supports complex hierarchical structures
Distributional regression (model σ, not just μ)
Custom families and link functions
Generates Stan code on the fly

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Installation:
install.packages("brms")
library(brms)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Basic Syntax:
# Standard regression
model <- brm(y ~ x, data = mydata)

# Hierarchical model
model <- brm(y ~ x + (1 | group), data = mydata)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
When to Use brms:

Need custom distributions
Complex random effects structures
Non-linear models
Want maximum flexibility

text:
Interpreting rstanarm Output
Output Looks Like:


Code
broom.mixed::tidy(partial_pool, conf.int = TRUE)


# A tibble: 4 × 6
  term                    estimate std.error conf.low conf.high group   
  <chr>                      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   
1 (Intercept)              3.43      0.314    2.90       3.98   <NA>    
2 length                   0.00563   0.00731 -0.00650    0.0172 <NA>    
3 sd_(Intercept).lake      0.804    NA       NA         NA      lake    
4 sd_Observation.Residual  0.383    NA       NA         NA      Residual


What This Means:
Fixed Effects:

Intercept = 3.4 µg/g: Average mercury for average-length fish
Length = 0.005: Each cm of length → 0.005 µg/g more mercury
95% CI [-0.07, 0.01]: No evidence of relationship

Random Effects:

SD(lake) = 0.8: Lakes differ by about 0.8 µg/g on average
SD(residual) = 0.4: Fish within lake differ by 0.4 µg/g
Between-lake variance > within-lake variance!

Conclusion: Lake identity matters more than individual variation!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Extracting and Reporting Results


Fixed Effects:
#| label: bayesian-hierarchical-13
# Get fixed effects summary
fixef(radon_model2)

# Get posterior samples
posterior_samples <- as_draws_df(radon_model2)

VarCorr(radon_model2)

# Extract county-specific effects

# Plot random effects distribution
mcmc_areas(radon_model2, pars = "sd_county__Intercept")

Reporting:

Fixed effects: median and 95% CI
Probability statements: P(β > 0 | data) = 0.97
Random effects: report SD and interpretation
Always include uncertainty!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Prior Selection for Hierarchical Models
Why Priors Matter:
In hierarchical models, priors are particularly important for:

Variance parameters (σ_α, σ_y)
Group-level effects with limited data
Complex models with many parameters

Default vs Custom Priors:
rstanarm Defaults (Usually Good):

Weakly informative
Scaled to data
Rarely need to change

brms Requires Specification:

More flexible
Should think about priors
Can use get_prior() to see options

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Prior Selection Guidelines
For Fixed Effects (β):
prior(normal(0, 5), class = b)

Normal(0, 5) is weakly informative
Allows wide range but not absurd values
Adjust scale based on response variable units

For Standard Deviations (σ):
prior(cauchy(0, 1), class = sigma)
prior(cauchy(0, 1), class = sd)

Half-Cauchy is standard choice
Heavy tails allow large values if data support it
Scale should relate to expected variation

For Correlations:
prior(lkj(2), class = cor)

LKJ prior for correlation matrices
η = 2 is weakly informative (favors no correlation)
η = 1 is uniform (all correlations equally likely)

Principle: Weakly informative priors that regularize but don’t dominate data

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Prior Sensitivity Analysis
Always Check Prior Influence:
# Fit with different priors
model_weak <- brm(
  y ~ x + (1 | group),
  prior = prior(normal(0, 10), class = b)
)

model_strong <- brm(
  y ~ x + (1 | group),
  prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = b)
)

# Compare posteriors
posterior_weak <- as_draws_df(model_weak)
posterior_strong <- as_draws_df(model_strong)

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(posterior_weak$b_x), color = "blue") +
  geom_density(aes(posterior_strong$b_x), color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Prior Sensitivity", subtitle = "Blue = Weak, Red = Strong")
What to Look For:

Are posteriors similar? Good! (Data overwhelms prior)
Very different? Prior is too strong OR insufficient data
If conclusions change: report sensitivity, get more data

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Example 3: Species Abundance Across Sites (rstanarm)
Scenario: Counting birds at 40 sites over 3 years
Data Structure:

Site (40 levels)
Year (3 levels)
Habitat type (forest, grassland, wetland)
Count data (Poisson distributed)

Question: How does habitat affect abundance? How much do sites vary?

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Example 3: Species Abundance Across Sites (rstanarm)
Model with Poisson Distribution:
library(rstanarm)

bird_model <- stan_glmer(
  count ~ habitat + (1 | site) + (1 | year),
  data = bird_data,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  seed = 123,
  refresh = 0
)

print(bird_model)
Key Features:

Poisson family for count data
Log link function (counts can’t be negative)
Two grouping factors: site AND year
Crossed random effects (not nested)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Example 3: Interpreting Count Model
Model Structure:
log(λ_ij) = β₀ + β₁×(habitat=grassland) + β₂×(habitat=wetland) 
            + α_site[i] + α_year[j]
count_ij ~ Poisson(λ_ij)
Output Interpretation:
Fixed Effects:
                    Estimate  95% CI
(Intercept)         2.3       [2.0, 2.6]
habitatgrassland    0.4       [0.2, 0.6]
habitatwetland      0.8       [0.5, 1.1]

Random Effects:
Groups  Name        Std.Dev.
site    (Intercept) 0.3
year    (Intercept) 0.1
What This Means:

exp(2.3) = 10: Expected count in forest
exp(2.3 + 0.4) = 15: Expected count in grassland
exp(2.3 + 0.8) = 25: Expected count in wetland
Sites vary by factor of exp(0.3×2) ≈ 1.8 (±2 SD)
Years vary by factor of exp(0.1×2) ≈ 1.2
Site variation larger than year variation

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Crossed vs Nested Random Effects


Nested: Groups within groups

Sites within regions
Students within schools
Plots within forests

# Syntax
(1 | region/site)
# or equivalently
(1 | region) + (1 | region:site)
Crossed: Independent grouping factors

Sites AND years (each site measured each year)
Subjects AND stimuli (each subject sees each stimulus)
Raters AND items (each rater rates each item)

# Syntax
(1 | site) + (1 | year)

How to Tell:

Nested: Each site belongs to exactly one region
Crossed: Each combination of site×year is possible

Environmental Examples:

Nested: Transects within sites within watersheds
Crossed: Sites measured across multiple years
Mixed: Sites within regions, measured across years

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Example 4: Varying Slopes (Environmental Gradient)
Scenario: Tree growth along elevation gradient at 15 sites
Question: Does elevation effect vary by site?


Random Intercepts Only:
model_ri <- brm(
  growth ~ elevation + (1 | site),
  data = tree_data,
  family = gaussian()
)

All sites: same elevation slope
Sites differ only in baseline growth


Random Intercepts and Slopes:
model_ris <- brm(
  growth ~ elevation + (1 + elevation | site),
  data = tree_data,
  family = gaussian()
)

Each site: own elevation slope
Sites differ in baseline AND relationship
Intercepts and slopes can be correlated

When to Use Random Slopes:

Theory suggests effect varies
Sufficient data per group
Interaction between group and predictor

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Interpreting Random Slopes Output
Model Output:
Random Effects:
~site (Number of levels: 15)
              Estimate Est.Error
sd(Intercept)    2.1      0.5
sd(elevation)    0.3      0.1
cor(Intercept,elevation) -0.4  0.2
What This Means:
sd(Intercept) = 2.1:

Sites vary in baseline growth by ±2.1 mm/year

sd(elevation) = 0.3:

Elevation slopes vary by ±0.3 across sites
Some sites more sensitive to elevation than others

cor(Intercept, elevation) = -0.4:

Negative correlation: sites with high baseline growth show weaker elevation effect
Low-elevation (high-baseline) sites less affected by going higher
High-elevation sites more affected by elevation changes

Interpretation: Sites show consistent but varying responses to elevation

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Predicting for New Groups
Major Advantage of Hierarchical Models:
Scenario: You want to predict mercury for a NEW, unsampled lake
Three Approaches:
1. Complete Pooling:

Use population average
Ignores that lakes differ
Underpredicts uncertainty

2. No Pooling:

Can’t predict! No data for this lake
Completely stuck

3. Partial Pooling (Hierarchical):

Use population distribution of lake effects
Incorporates uncertainty about new lake
This works!

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Predicting for New Groups (Code)


Generate Predictions:


Code
# Create data for new lake
new_lake_data <- data.frame(
  lake = "Lake_NEW", # Previously unobserved
  length = seq(10, 40, by = 5)
)

# Predict allowing new levels
predictions <- posterior_predict(
  partial_pool,
  newdata = new_lake_data,
  allow_new_levels = TRUE
)

# Summarize predictions
pred_summary <- new_lake_data %>%
  mutate(
    median = apply(predictions, 2, median),
    lower = apply(predictions, 2, quantile, 0.05),
    upper = apply(predictions, 2, quantile, 0.95)
  )

# Plot
ggplot(pred_summary, aes(x = length)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median)) +
  labs(title = "Predictions for New Lake", y = "Mercury (µg/g)") +
  theme_minimal()










What Happens:

Model samples new lake effect from population distribution
Wider intervals than for observed lakes (more uncertainty)
Uses all available information about population

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)
What is ICC?
Proportion of total variance due to grouping structure.
Formula:
ICC = σ²_group / (σ²_group + σ²_residual)
Interpretation:

ICC = 0: Grouping doesn’t matter (no clustering)
ICC = 0.05: 5% of variance is between groups
ICC = 0.50: Half of variance is between groups
ICC = 1.0: All variance is between groups

Practical Meaning:

High ICC: Groups are very different, group identity is important
Low ICC: Groups are similar, might not need hierarchical model
ICC > 0.05: Generally use hierarchical model

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)
In R:
# Calculate ICC
performance::icc(model)

# Or manually from output
var_group <- 0.8^2  # SD of group effect
var_resid <- 0.3^2  # Residual SD
icc <- var_group / (var_group + var_resid)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Variance Partitioning
Where Does Variation Come From?
Example: Multi-Level Environmental Study
Total Variation = Region + Site-within-Region + Measurement
From Model:
Random Effects:
 Groups           Variance  Proportion
 region           2.5       0.45 (45%)
 site:region      1.8       0.32 (32%)
 Residual         1.3       0.23 (23%)
 Total            5.6
Interpretation:

Most variation (45%) is between regions
Site differences account for 32%
Within-site variation is 23%
Implications: Regional factors most important!

Management Implications:

Focus monitoring at regional level
Site-specific interventions less important
Within-site variation relatively small
Invest resources in understanding regional drivers

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Model Selection and Comparison
How to Choose Between Models?

Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOO)WAIC (Watanabe-Akaike IC):Bayes Factor (for nested models)


# Compute LOO for each model
loo1 <- loo(model1)
loo2 <- loo(model2)

# Compare
loo_compare(loo1, loo2)

ELPD = Expected Log Pointwise Predictive Density
Higher ELPD = Better
Difference > 2×SE suggests meaningful difference



waic(model1)
waic(model2)

Lower WAIC = Better
Similar to LOO but different computation



library(bridgesampling)
bf <- bayes_factor(model1, model2)

Ratio of marginal likelihoods
BF > 10: Strong evidence for model1

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Model Selection: Practical Considerations
Don’t Rely Only on Metrics!
Consider:

Scientific Plausibility

Does model make sense?
Consistent with theory?

Interpretability

Can you explain results?
Simpler is often better

Predictive Performance

How well does it predict new data?
Check posterior predictive checks

Computational Feasibility

Does it converge?
Reasonable run time?

Robustness

Sensitive to priors?
Stable across subsets?


Best Practice: Fit multiple reasonable models, compare, report sensitivity

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Common Pitfalls and Solutions
1. Convergence Failures

Problem: Rhat > 1.1, divergent transitions
Solutions:

Run more iterations
Reparameterize model
Use stronger priors
Check for multicollinearity


2. Too Many Random Effects

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Example Write-Up
Methods:
“We fit a Bayesian hierarchical linear model with random intercepts for lakes to account for repeated measures within lakes. The model included fish length as a fixed effect. We used weakly informative priors: Normal(0, 5) for fixed effects and Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5) for variance parameters. We fit the model using stan_glmer from the rstanarm package with 4 chains of 2000 iterations each (1000 warmup). Convergence was assessed using Rhat statistics (all < 1.01) and visual inspection of trace plots.”
Results:
“Fish length had a positive effect on mercury concentration (β = 0.52, 95% CI [0.34, 0.71], P(β > 0) > 0.999), with each additional cm associated with 0.52 µg/g more mercury. Lakes varied substantially in baseline mercury (SD = 0.78, 95% CI [0.53, 1.15]), with the intraclass correlation coefficient indicating that 58% of total variance was attributable to differences between lakes. Posterior predictive checks indicated good model fit (Figure S1).”

When Relationships Aren’t Linear:


# Non-linear growth curve
nl_model <- brm(
  bf(
    height ~ a * (1 - exp(-k * age)),
    a ~ 1 + (1 | species),
    k ~ 1 + (1 | species),
    nl = TRUE
  ),
  data = growth_data,
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(100, 20), nlpar = "a"),
    prior(normal(0.1, 0.05), nlpar = "k", lb = 0)
  )
)

Growth curves (von Bertalanffy, logistic)

Michaelis-Menten kinetics
Population dynamics

Species/site-specific parameters

Advanced Topics: Distributional Regression
Model More Than the Mean:


# Model both mean AND variance
dist_model <- brm(
  bf(
    mercury ~ length + (1 | lake),
    sigma ~ length + (1 | lake)
  ),
  data = fish_data,
  family = gaussian()
)

What This Does:

Mean mercury depends on length and lake
Variance ALSO depends on length and lake
Some lakes more variable than others
Variability might increase with length (heteroscedasticity)

Applications:

When variance differs across groups
Heteroscedasticity
Understanding variability patterns
Risk assessment (variance matters!)

2. Specify Model

Random intercepts, slopes, or both?
Fixed effects of interest

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Complete Workflow Example (Code)
library(rstanarm)
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesplot)

# 1. Explore data structure
summary(mydata)
table(mydata$site)  # How many obs per site?

# 2. Fit model
model <- stan_glmer(
  response ~ predictor1 + predictor2 + (1 + predictor1 | site),
  data = mydata,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  seed = 123
)

# 3. Check convergence
summary(model)  # Look at Rhat
mcmc_trace(model, pars = c("(Intercept)", "predictor1", "predictor2"))

# 4. Posterior predictive check
pp_check(model, type = "dens_overlay", ndraws = 50)

# 5. Extract results
fixef(model)
ranef(model)
performance::icc(model)

# 6. Visualize
plot(model)
mcmc_areas(model, pars = c("predictor1", "predictor2"))

# 7. Predict
new_data <- expand.grid(
  predictor1 = seq(min(mydata$predictor1), max(mydata$predictor1), length = 100),
  predictor2 = mean(mydata$predictor2),
  site = "Site1"
)
predictions <- posterior_epred(model, newdata = new_data)

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
section: Decision Guide: When to Use What
text:
Decision Guide: When to Use What
Use Standard Regression When: - No clustering or repeated measures - All observations truly independent - Single level of observation
Use Hierarchical Model When: - Nested or grouped data structure - Repeated measures - Unbalanced group sizes - Want to generalize to new groups - Interested in group-level variation
Use Random Intercepts When: - Groups differ in baseline/mean - Same relationship across groups - Most common hierarchical model
Use Random Slopes When: - Relationship varies by group - Sufficient data per group (n ≥ 5-10) - Theoretical reason to expect variation
Use rstanarm When: - Want simple, standard models - Getting started with Bayesian - Need fast computation
Use brms When: - Need flexibility - Complex random effects - Custom distributions - Distributional regression

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Summary: Key Takeaways
Core Concepts: 1. Clustering matters: Ignoring structure leads to wrong conclusions 2. Partial pooling: Best of complete and no pooling approaches 3. Shrinkage: Automatic regularization toward population mean 4. Information sharing: Small groups borrow strength from larger groups
Practical Benefits: - Correct standard errors - Better predictions for groups with little data - Can predict for new, unobserved groups - Explicitly models and estimates sources of variation - Handles unbalanced data elegantly
When to Use: - Nested/grouped/repeated measures data - Interest in group-level variation - Predictions for new groups - Unbalanced sample sizes - Common in environmental science!
Bayesian Advantages: - Natural hierarchical framework - Handles small samples well - Full uncertainty quantification - Direct probability statements - Flexible and extensible

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Common Questions
Q: How many groups/observations per group do I need? - Minimum: ~5-10 groups for stable variance estimates - Per group: 2-3 minimum, 5-10 ideal for random slopes - Unbalanced is OK! (that’s a strength of hierarchical models)
Q: Random or fixed effects? - Fixed: Specific levels you care about (e.g., specific treatments) - Random: Sample from population, want to generalize - If unsure: start with random, it’s usually safer
Q: How do I know if I need random slopes? - Theory suggests varying relationships - Test with model comparison (LOO/WAIC) - Plot data by group—do slopes look different? - Need enough data per group
Q: Do I need to worry about p-values? - No! Use credible intervals and probability statements - P(β > 0 | data) is more interpretable than p-value - Focus on effect sizes and uncertainty
Q: How do I deal with convergence problems? - Run more iterations - Use informative priors - Reparameterize model - Check for multicollinearity

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
Additional Resources
Books: - “Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models” - Gelman & Hill - “Statistical Rethinking” - McElreath (Bayesian focused) - “Bayesian Data Analysis” - Gelman et al. (advanced) - “Hierarchical Modeling for Environmental Sciences” - Clark & Gelfand
Online Resources: - Stan documentation - rstanarm vignettes - brms documentation - Michael Clark’s Mixed Models tutorial
R Packages: - rstanarm: Simple Bayesian hierarchical models - brms: Flexible Bayesian hierarchical models - bayesplot: Visualization for Bayesian models - tidybayes: Tidy manipulation of Bayesian output - performance: Model diagnostics including ICC
Practice Datasets: - Radon data (rstanarm package) - sleepstudy (lme4 package) - Environmental datasets in lterdatasampler

title: Advanced: Bayesian Hierarchical Models
text:
End of Slide Deck
Next Steps:

Start with simple random intercepts models
Use your own data with grouping structure
Check convergence and model fit carefully
Gradually add complexity (random slopes, predictors)
Compare to non-hierarchical models to see the difference
Practice interpreting variance components

Key Principles: - Respect the structure in your data - Partial pooling is usually the right answer - Bayesian framework is natural for hierarchical models - Always check convergence and model fit - Visualize random effects to understand patterns - Report uncertainty honestly
Remember: - Hierarchical models are appropriate for most environmental data - They provide better estimates and correct inference - rstanarm and brms make fitting these models straightforward - The hardest part is understanding the concept, not the code!
Good luck with your hierarchical modeling!

title: Lecture 2
text:
History
The ideas behind visual EDA dates back over 100 years

Arthur Lyon Bowley, one of the early statisticians, used precursors of the stemplot and the five-number summary, using instead a seven-number summary (maximum, minimum, median, quartiles and two deciles)
The modern concept of EDA traces back to John Tukey’s seminal book Exploratory Data Analysis (1977), based on his work at the famous Bell Labs.


Exploratory data analysis can never be the whole story, but nothing else can serve as the foundation stone –- as the first step
John Tukey, 1977

Bowley, A.L (1920). Elementary Manual of Statistics, 3rd Edition

title: Lecture 2
text:
A more modern description

An approach/philosophy for data analysis that employs a variety of techniques (mostly graphical) to maximize insight into a data set, uncover underlying structure, extract important variables, detect outliers and anomalies, test underlying assumptions, develop parsimonious models and determine optimal factor settings.
U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology


 Being able to interpret what you see in question-agnostic visualizations
 Using visualizations to ask particular questions of the data (but beware of biases in your questions and approach)
 Synthesize what you find into confirmatory approaches (expository figures, models, hypotheses, validation)
 Gain awareness of data characteristics that may modify or bias your interpretations or inferences (informative missingness, collinearity, pattern changes)


EDA is the first process (not just a step) to go through after receiving a data set

Allows us to understand univariate, bivariate and multivariate patterns
Allows us to quickly catch issues and mistakes in the data
Allows us to start to hypothesize about potential analyses
Allows us to ensure that the data aligns with the context (the science or the business case)
Hopefully prevents us from going down unreasonable analytic paths

Almost entirely graphical

People catch graphical anomalies much faster than textual anomalies
We inherently can recognize patterns

title: Lecture 2
section: Cognitive biases can affect our EDA
text:
Cognitive biases can affect our EDA

EDA is about interpreting what is evident in the data and seeing how the data answers questions we ask of it.

Several known cognitive biases can affect how we understand the results of an EDA:

Confirmation bias

We look for and find what we want to see. This is especially insidious. One way to handle this is to look at question-agnostic visualizations and make honest interpretations of what we see

Selection bias

Selecting a particular subset of the data to look at, rather than all the data

Anchoring bias

The tendency to rely on the first piece of information we see

Framing bias

The tendency to be influenced by how the information is presented rather than the actual information itself (applicable to white hat/black hat)


Other biases

title: Lecture 2
text:
Combating confirmation bias
Question Formulation
Frame neutral, open-ended questions instead of leading ones that validate existing beliefs. For example, ask “How are ticket sales distributed across the week?” rather than “Are sales higher on weekends?”
Structured Approach
Clear Objectives: Define specific, achievable goals at the project’s outset to maintain focus and avoid selectively interpreting data to fit predetermined narratives
Multiple Hypotheses: Test multiple competing hypotheses rather than seeking to prove a single assumption. Structure hypotheses to test if your assumptions are wrong, not that they are correct
Analysis Methods
Diverse Data Sources: Seek out multiple data sources that can complement, contrast, or challenge your initial findings
Systematic Tools: Utilize analytical tools and statistical methods to process data objectively, making the analysis more transparent and reproducible
Collaborative Practices
Peer Review: Engage colleagues with impartial views to review your data, methods, and conclusions
Fresh Perspectives: Consider having a different team examine the data and results with fresh eyes to identify potential biases the original team might have missed[8].
Documentation
Record Keeping: Document your analysis steps, assumptions, and decisions throughout the exploration phase
Transparent Limitations: Explicitly identify the strengths and limitations of your analysis before starting, and be clear about any potential conflicts of interest[6].
Best Practices
Active Search: Deliberately look for evidence that contradicts your initial hypotheses rather than just supporting data
Early Feedback: Debrief with stakeholders to avoid misinterpretation of results and preempt biased follow-up requests

title: Lecture 2
section: Why are missing data patterns important
text:
Why are missing data patterns important

From a completeness perspective, it gives a sense of the amount of usable data on hand
From an analytic perspective, there’s actually a bit more

A fundamental idea in handling missing data is that the missingness happens at random
If the missingness is at random, we can ignore it for the purposes of analysis and modeling
If it isn’t at random, it’s considered informative or non-ignorable missingness and has to be dealt with analytically, either via imputation or as an explicit component in any modeling strategy
If some variables tend to be missing together, it points to flaws in the data collection process as well as an issue with correlated missingness.
If some variables have “too much” missing, should we consider tossing them?



Informative missingness: basically, can the missing status predict other characteristics of the individuals to some degree of certainty

Pregnant (Y/N) and males are coded as missing
data from particular labs are missing, or much more likely to be missing
Sicker people miss hospital visits

Tossing a variable needs to be very carefully considered. It is a last resort
We think about possible imputation strategies if we have 10-30% missing, especially if another variable is well-correlated with it
Sometimes we still keep it in and do a subgroup analysis, because that variable is important to understanding but hard to collect

Some kinds of non-standard blood components
expensive PET scans
differences in facilities across countries

Still we need to think about whether the missingness is informative and account for it

title: Lecture 2
text:
A missing data typography

Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)

The fact that data are missing is independent of the observed and unobserved data, i.e. no systematic difference exist between subject with and without missing data

Missing at Random (MAR)

The fact that the data are missing is systematically related to data we observe but not to the underlying values of the unobserved data

Missing Not at Random (MNAR)

The fact that the data are missing is systematically related to the values of the unobserved data. In other words, you are in neither the MCAR or MAR situations


Consider a dataset with the following three variables: disease status, level of exposure, and age. Suppose, for some individuals, exposure is missing.

MCAR: Any two individuals, regardless of their values of disease status, level of exposure, and age, have the same probability of having a missing value for exposure.
MAR: Any two individuals with the same disease status and age have the same chance of having a missing exposure value, regardless of how large or small their actual level of exposure.
MNAR: Even among individuals with the same disease status and age, the chance of having a missing exposure value depends on the level of exposure.

title: Lecture 2
text:
UpSet plots
The UpSet plot was originally developed at Harvard in 2014.
The main purpose was to solve the problem of set visualizations when you have more than one set (so an extension of Venn Diagrams), in an intuitive manner

It tries to solve the problem created by the following visualization looking at the intersection of 6 sets



D’Hont et al, The banana (Musa acuminata) genome and the evolution of monocotyledonous plants. Nature 488, 213-217 (2012)




We can use Venn diagrams to understand co-occurrences or common elements in 2 or 3 sets. But what do we do if we want to compare more than 3 sets.
There are solutions like Euler diagrams, but they tend to take a bit of contortion to understand, much like the banana figure.
UpSet plots offer a more intuitive solution

title: Lecture 4
text:
What is Pattern Recognition?

A branch of machine learning focused on classifying data or detecting structures in datasets.

Rooted in statistics and mathematical models.

Goal: Build models to identify trends, predict outcomes, or group data meaningfully.

title: Lecture 4
text:
Major Approaches

Supervised Learning: Model learns from labeled examples.

Unsupervised Learning: Model detects hidden structures without labels.

Often blends statistical modeling (probability theory) with computational optimization.

title: Lecture 4
section: The goal is to find patterns in the data
text:
The goal is to find patterns in the data

The idea here is to use potentially complex models to reflect underlying patterns in the data
Which of the paradigms do you think this falls into, predictive or inferential?

title: Lecture 4
section: Let’s talk about the two worlds
text:
Let’s talk about the two worlds

Breiman is a bit strident in his condemnation of the data model in favor of machine learning
ISLR has a more balanced view
Two main objectives, and you need to decide going in which one you want to hit

Prediction - can I understand this data in hand well enough to get a handle on what will happen with new data
Inference - can I understand why the patterns in the data are the way they are




Inferential approaches lead to causal approaches, predictive approaches do not in general

title: Lecture 4
text:
Statistical models vs machine learning
We will be using both statistical models and machine learning models in this class

Statistical models like linear regression, logistic regression etc are also used for machine learning purposes

So you may be a bit confused. Always understand the purpose of the model to understand the analytic approach

title: Lecture 4
text:
A general paradigm

Training on input-output pairs:

Input: feature vector \(x\)
Output: label \(y\)

Goal: Learn mapping \[f(x) \approx y\]
We play around with the functional form of \(f\)

In statistical models we specify the functional form of \(f\)
In machine learning the machine learns the functional form of \(f\) within some imposed constraints








What are the implications of this?


Especially in terms of data volume and signal to noise ratios

title: Lecture 4
text:
The linear model
Here we model
\[
y = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 +...+error
\]






Linear in parameters, not shape


The linear model is a linear function of \(b_0, b_1, b_2, ..\). The predictors can basically be anything, including transformations of the original data
For example,
\[
y = b_0 + b_1x_1 + error
\]
\[
y = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_1^2 + error
\]
\[
y = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3 x_1x_2
\]
are all linear models

section: So what’s going on with geom_smooth?
text:
So what’s going on with geom_smooth?
geom_smooth uses machine learning to fit a locally representative curve to the data

It creates windows on the x-axis and finds the best estimate of y (typically the mean)
As the window moves, it computes the mean of y for each window and then joins them in a curve

title: Lecture 4
text:
Supervised Learning

Training on input-output pairs:

Input: feature vector \(x\)
Output: label \(y\)

Goal: Learn mapping \[f(x) \approx y\]
Applications:

Spam detection

Medical diagnosis

Weather forecasting

Predicting customers

title: Lecture 4
text:
But…
Now, instead of finding the best-fitting curve, it finds the curve that best predicts on new data.

title: Lecture 4
text:
Judging different models

Statistical models are typically judged by the quality of the fit on the current data

Using the mean-square error \[\sum(y - f(x))^2\]

Predictive models are judged by how well it predicts on data it hasn’t seen yet.

Still using mean-square error, but using new data

title: Lecture 4
text:
The supervised learning approach

Split your data up into 2 parts
Fit your model to one part (called the training data)
Now judge your model on the other part (called the test or validation data)

Or you can get new data that is similar to the training data

title: Lecture 4
text:
More generally, we use cross-validation

We’ll then average the performance over all the validation sets to judge the model

title: Lecture 4
text:
What’s the point?

Finding better models in a predictive sense
Trying to minimize the generalizability error
Getting to a model you can hopefully trust to understand the world

Training on unlabeled data:

Only input vector \(x\), no predefined labels.


Goal: Discover structure or patterns.

title: Lecture 4
text:
Bias-Variance Tradeoff

A central concept in statistical learning.

Bias: Error due to overly simple models (underfitting).

Variance: Error due to overly complex models reacting to noise (overfitting).

Goal: Find the sweet spot minimizing total error.

Underfitting: High bias, low variance

Overfitting: Low bias, high variance

Best models balance the two for optimal generalization.

text:
Which models work (in this sense)?

Linear models (as in a straight line model) will often underfit
Neural networks will often overfit if not careful
Hybrid methods that fit a lot of simple models together seem to work well

Random Forests
Boosted Trees

text:

Deep learning is a class of neural networks
They have many layers that can capture minute patterns in the data

title: Lecture 4

Statistical Pattern Recognition in Practice

Requires:

Clear problem definition

Choice of features or dimensionality reduction

Model selection (based on complexity and interpretability)

Evaluation with test/train splits or cross-validation

title: Lecture 4
text:
Key Takeaways

Pattern recognition blends statistics with machine learning.

Supervised learning uses labels; unsupervised learning finds structure.

The bias-variance tradeoff is crucial for balancing model complexity and predictive accuracy.

title: Lecture 6
section: The Gaussian distribution is not so important in practice
text:
The Gaussian distribution is not so important in practice

Classical statistics relies on the Gaussian distribution (through the Central Limit Theorem) to make inference around means

Most things we look at are in fact means or averages. A proportion is the average number of 1’s we see.

Simulation methods don’t require many assumptions and reflect the data we see much better

We’ll try to get simulated results rather than make assumptions on probability distributions that aren’t verifiable
The simulations do make the assumptions we make quite explicit.
You can use simulations to understand properties of “non-standard” statistics

title: Lecture 6
text:
Some definitions

Population

The full set of individuals/observations that are under investigation

Sample

A subset of the population that is actually observed (the definition of sample is context dependent and doesn’t have to be random)

Random sample

A sample where each individual/event in the population has an equal chance of being selected

Parameter

A numerical summary of a population (e.g., population mean, population proportion); some characteristic of interest

Statistic

A numerical summary of a sample (e.g., sample mean, sample proportion)

title: Lecture 6
text:
Study 1
What is the average amount of PM2.5 particles at Reagan National Airport in August, 2025?

Population: PM2.5 readings at all times in August, 2025
Sample: Daily readings at 9am, 12 noon, and 5pm during August 2025
Parameter: Average PM2.5 readings (\(\mu\)) during August, 2025 (unobservable)
Statistic (corresponding to the parameter): Average of the PM2.5 levels (\(\bar{x}\)) observed during August, 2025



Questions


Is this study based on a random sample?
Are there evident biases in the results we might get from this study?

title: Lecture 6
text:
Study 2
What is the median income of people in the District of Columbia?

Population: Incomes of all people in DC
Sample: Asking 50 individuals on the Georgetown Campus
Parameter: Median income of people in DC
Statistic: Median income of people in the sample



Questions


What are the issues with the sample in this study?
Would you trust your results to answer the question you’re addressing?
Can we do better?

title: Lecture 6
text:
Revisiting the Central Limit Theorem
Here’s the formal definition:

Suppose \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) is a random sample from some population distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Then, as \(n \rightarrow \infty\),
\[
\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \rightarrow^d N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
\]
i.e., the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal (Gaussian) distribution as \(n \rightarrow \infty\).

So, what’s a sampling distribution? And how is this theorem useful for understanding something about \(\mu\)?

title: Lecture 6
text:
The population distribution
The population distribution is the distribution of observations of interest in the population

title: Lecture 6
text: A random sample (of size n=50)

title: Lecture 6
text:
The sample distribution
The sampling distribution of the mean (or any statistic) is the distribution of the statistic over all possible random samples of size n from the population.

Of course for any real situation, we don’t have access to all possible samples, since it’s often prohibitively expensive to collect data
But we can approximate this distribution through simulation

Draw n samples from the population repeatedly
Calculate the statistic of interest for each sample (here, the mean)
Plot the distribution of these statistics

title: Lecture 6
section: Simulating the sampling distribution of the mean

title: Lecture 6
section: Simulating the sampling distribution of the mean
text:
Simulating the sampling distribution of the mean


Simulation code
set.seed(123)
n_sims <- 1000
n <- 50
sample_means <- replicate(n_sims, {
  sample_n(dc_pop, size = n) |>
    summarise(mean_age = mean(age)) |>
    pull(mean_age)
})

tibble(sample_mean = sample_means) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_textvline(
    xintercept = mean(dc_pop$age),
    label = 'Population mean',
    hjust = 0.2,
    color = 'red4',
    linetype = 'dashed',
    size = 4,
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = glue::glue("Sampling distribution of the sample mean (n={n})"),
    x = "Sample mean of age",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  lims(x = c(28, 45)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20))









Notice that the population mean is pretty much in the middle of the sampling distribution. This is an application of the CLT.

title: Lecture 6
text:
Uncertainty in the sample mean
It’s clear that the sample mean varies from sample to sample. This is called sampling variability. But how much does it vary?






Terminology


The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is called the standard error (SE) of the sample mean, and is given by: \[
SE(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\] where \(\sigma\) is the population standard deviation.



Now the CLT gives us a bit of a guarantee based on properties of the normal distribution.


About 68% of the time, the sample mean will be within 1 SE of the population mean
About 95% of the time, the sample mean will be within 2 SE of the population mean
About 99.7% of the time, the sample mean will be within 3 SE of the population mean

title: Lecture 6
section: A word about the standard deviation
text:
A word about the standard deviation
The SD is a measure of how much the data varies.
\[
\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\bar{x})^2
\]
is called the variance. It is measuring how far from the mean, on average, we might see observations.

Higher values of \(\sigma\) means a wider range of possible observable values, and a “fatter” histogram

title: Lecture 6
text:
Code
library(ggdist)
library(distributional)
tibble(sigma=seq(0.5, 3, by=0.5)) |>
    ggplot(aes(y=sigma, xdist = dist_normal(0,sigma))) +
        stat_halfeye() +
        labs(x = "Normal(0, sigma) distribution", y = 'sigma')

title: Lecture 6
section: Smaller SE means we’re closer to the truth
text:
Smaller SE means we’re closer to the truth

The smaller the SE, the tighter the sampling distribution is around the true (unobservable) parameter

It is more likely that your sample mean is within some small interval of the truth


\[
\Pr(-c < \bar{X}_n - \mu < c) \rightarrow 1\quad\text{as}\quad n\rightarrow \infty
\]
for any positive number c






But we only observe finite n


So, we need to have an idea of how close we might be for a given n, or what n would get us “close enough”

title: Lecture 6
text:
Bounding uncertainty
Recall that for a normal distribution, you have a 95% likelihood of being within 2 SE of the mean
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
0.95 &=& \Pr(\mu - 2\sigma/\sqrt{n} < \bar{X}_n < \mu + 2 \sigma/\sqrt{n})\\
&=& \Pr(\bar{X}_n - 2\sigma/\sqrt{n} < \mu < \bar{X}_n + 2 \sigma/\sqrt{n})
\end{eqnarray}
\]
This doesn’t get us quite there, since we also don’t know the true value of \(\sigma\), but this is saying that…

the true mean will be within \(\bar{X}_n \pm 2\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) 95% of the time.
We can’t quite say that. What is random here? The interval, not the parameter (Huh?!!)

But we will be able to say something like this when we talk about Bayesian statistics

title: Lecture 6
text: The variable interval of uncertainty

title: Lecture 6
text:
We can make mistakes …
and we won’t know if we make one!!!

Statistics is all about using probability to give us limits to how often we might be wrong (yes, “uncertainty” pops its head again)
Uncertainty intervals like this are a thing even in machine learning, when you have limited training data
What we’re doing is inferring something about our world with partial information, and so our inference will be imperfect.


What can we say about this interval we would create from one sample that is in hand

Intervals constructed in this manner from repeated samples would cover the true mean 95% of the time.
We don’t, and will never, know whether the particular interval we got covers the true mean

Rather unsatisfying, right?

title: Lecture 6
text:
The confidence interval
What we developed in the past few slides is called a confidence interval, in particular a 95% confidence interval.

The 95% comes from the choice of \(\pm\) 2 SE that we made. A different factor would give a different confidence level.
You can set that factor by using qnorm((1-p)/2, lower.tail=FALSE) where p is the confidence level you want as a decimal



The confidence interval is widely used in practice, and is often reported in papers and articles
It does give us a sense of how uncertain we are about our estimate of the parameter
But it is often misinterpreted as a probability statement about the parameter, i.e., that there’s a 95% chance the parameter lies in the interval we got

title: Lecture 6
section: Computing a confidence interval in the real world
text:
Computing a confidence interval in the real world
One thing we glossed over is that we don’t know \(\sigma\) in practice!
We can estimate it from the sample using the sample standard deviation \(s\): \[
s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2
\] This gives us the estimated standard error: \[
SE(\bar{X}) \approx \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\] We can then construct the confidence interval as: \[
\bar{X} \pm 2 \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
But, since we’re estimating \(\sigma\) here from a sample, and that estimate has sampling variability, the \(\pm\) 2 SE won’t quite give us the right coverage.

title: Lecture 6
text:
The t-distribution to the rescue
When we estimate \(\sigma\) from a sample, the distribution of the sample mean (appropriately standardized) follows a t-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom
\[
\frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}
\]
So, we can use quantiles1 from the t-distribution instead of the normal distribution to get the right coverage.






Degrees of freedom


The degrees of freedom is the number of independent pieces of information that went into estimating a parameter. Here, we estimated \(\sigma\) from \(n\) observations, but since we also estimated \(\mu\) from the same \(n\) observations, we lost one degree of freedom. So, we have \(n-1\) degrees of freedom left to estimate \(\sigma\).



Quantiles are the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF). For a given probability p, the p-th quantile is the value x such that \(P(X \leq x) = p\).

title: Lecture 6
text:
The t-distribution
The t-distribution is similar to the normal distribution, but has heavier tails (is fatter), which accounts for the extra uncertainty introduced by estimating \(\sigma\).

title: Lecture 6
text:
Hypothesis testing
Stating hypotheses and finding evidence to support or refute them is central to the scientific method.

Understand that we will very rarely “prove” something, but rather will find a preponderance of evidence for or against a hypothesis
We’re used to the courtroom analogy of “beyond a reasonable doubt” or “preponderance of evidence”. Statistical hypothesis testing is similar.
We will use data to make decisions about the validity of hypotheses
We will use probability to quantify the strength of evidence, so quantify what “reasonable doubt” means
We will make decisions based on this evidence, but will always be aware that we might be wrong

title: Lecture 6
section: Distinguishing between estimation and hypothesis testing
text:
Distinguishing between estimation and hypothesis testing

Estimation is about finding a plausible value for a parameter, along with a measure of uncertainty (confidence interval)
Hypothesis testing is about making a decision about the validity of a hypothesis about a parameter, based on evidence from data
Both use the same underlying principles of probability and sampling distributions
Both are subject to sampling variability and uncertainty

title: Lecture 6
text:
Hypotheses in the statistical context
We usually state hypotheses in terms of parameters and values that they might take.
For example, if we are interested in the average age of people in DC, we might state:

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): \(\mu = 35\) (the average age is 35)
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)): \(\mu > 35\) (the average age is more than 35)

or

Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)): \(\mu \neq 35\) (the average age is not 35)

title: Lecture 6
text:
The null and alternative hypotheses

The null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is a statement of no effect or no difference. It is the hypothesis that we will test against.

It is a strawman that we will try to disprove or reject based on evidence from data

The alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)) is a statement of effect or difference. It is what we hope to find evidence for.


The one-sided nature of classical hypothesis testing

In classical hypothesis testing, we can only find evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We can never “accept” the null hypothesis. So we are trying to set up a strawman (\(H_0\)) to knock down. In reality, we set up the null hypothesis to be the opposite of what we want to find evidence for, or what we think is true and want to confirm.

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing
We will make errors in our decisions when we test hypotheses.

If the null hypothesis is true, we might still decide to reject it. This is called a Type I error (false positive).
If the null hypothesis is false, we might decide not to reject it. This is called a Type II error (false negative).

Those errors are asking,

“How unlikely is it to see data like this if the null hypothesis were true?” (Type I), and
“How likely is it to see data like this if the null hypothesis were false?” (Type II)

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing
In the sequel, we will use idealized distributions to illustrate concepts, based on the CLT. We’ll see that in practice, we can use resampling methods to get at the same ideas.
Let’s go to DC and take a random sample of 100 people and measure their ages.


Code
set.seed(1234)
n <- 100
sample_100 <- sample_n(dc_pop, n)
sample_100$age


  [1] 67 31 30 17 36 33 43 28 32 24 19 29 48 27 39 23 26 82 31 36 32 18  5 56 70
 [26] 47 35 55 21 59 38 50 59 19 30 60 35 27 19 73 44 25 59 25 34 63 31  3 70 32
 [51] 81 27 66 30 33 59 24 37 47  4 53 13 43 77 39 31 20 52 23 42 16 57 47 49 26
 [76] 28 63 60 14 33  3 54 56  5 29 18 19 40 35 49 84 60 82 60 76  0 43 68 27 26


This sample has a mean age of 39.23 and a standard deviation of 19.98. We know from earlier that the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal with mean \(\mu\) and standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing
We will test the hypotheses:

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): \(\mu = 35\) (the average age is 35)
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)): \(\mu > 35\) (the average age is more than 35)

We’ll deal with the Type I error first, i.e., how likely is it to see a sample mean as large as we saw if the null hypothesis were true?


Code
p = pnorm(mean(sample_100$age), mean = 35, sd = sd(dc_pop$age)/sqrt(n), lower.tail=FALSE)

tibble(group = 1, mean = 35, sd = sd(dc_pop$age)/sqrt(n)) |> 
ggplot(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), fill = stat(x > mean(sample_100$age))), show.legend=F) +
    stat_halfeye() + 
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE"='red', "FALSE" = 'lightblue')) +
    annotate('text', x = 40, y = 0.4, label = paste("p =", round(p,4)), size = 3) +
    labs(x = 'Age') + 
    theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = 'none')

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing
We see that the probability of seeing a sample mean as large as we saw if the null hypothesis were true is 0.019. This is called the p-value.

The p-value is the probability of observing data as extreme or more extreme than what we observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
We set a threshold called the significance level (\(\alpha\)), which is the maximum acceptable probability of making a Type I error.


This is where the “beyond a reasonable doubt” or “preponderance of evidence” comes in. How small does the p-value need to be for us to reject the null hypothesis?

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing
We decide on a significance level (\(\alpha\)) before we look at the data. A common choice is \(\alpha = 0.05\).
Once we see the data, we compare the p-value to \(\alpha\), and our work is basically done.
We might like to also take a look at the other kind of error, the Type II error.

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing: Errors
To understand the Type II error, we need to consider what happens if the null hypothesis is false. For our hypotheses, there is a range of possible true values for \(\mu\) that are greater than 35. The further away the true \(\mu\) is from 35, the easier it is to reject the null hypothesis, since the sample mean is likely to be larger.


Code
mu1 = 35; mu2 = 41; sdev = sd(dc_pop$age)/sqrt(n)
tibble(x = seq(28, 48, length.out=100)) |> 
    mutate(y1 = dnorm(x, mu1, sdev), y2 = dnorm(x, mu2, sdev)) |> 
ggplot(aes(x=x)) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mu1, sd = sdev), color = 'blue', size=1) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mu2, sd = sdev), color = 'red', size=1) +
    labs(x = 'Age') + 
    annotate('text', x = 35, y = 0.21, label = 'Null hypothesis', color = 'blue') +
    annotate('text', x = 43, y = 0.21, label = 'Alternative hypothesis', color = 'red') +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mean(sample_100$age), linetype = 2) +
    annotate('text', x = mean(sample_100$age)+1, y = 0.25, label = 'Observed sample mean', color = 'black', hjust = 0) +
    theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = 'none')

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing: Errors
To understand the Type II error, we need to consider what happens if the null hypothesis is false. For our hypotheses, there is a range of possible true values for \(\mu\) that are greater than 35. The further away the true \(\mu\) is from 35, the easier it is to reject the null hypothesis, since the sample mean is likely to be larger.

Concepts of hypothesis testing: Errors
To understand the Type II error, we need to consider what happens if the null hypothesis is false. For our hypotheses, there is a range of possible true values for \(\mu\) that are greater than 35. The further away the true \(\mu\) is from 35, the easier it is to reject the null hypothesis, since the sample mean is likely to be larger.


Code

tibble(x = seq(28, 48, length.out=100)) |>

    labs(x = 'Age') + 
    annotate('text', x = 35, y = 0.21, label = 'Null hypothesis', color = 'blue') +
    annotate('text', x = 43, y = 0.21, label = 'Alternative hypothesis', color = 'red') +
    annotate('text', x = 35, y = 0.02, hjust=1, label = 'Type II error', color = 'red') +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mean(sample_100$age), linetype = 2) +
    annotate('text', x = mean(sample_100$age)+1, y = 0.25, label = 'Observed sample mean', color = 'black', hjust = 0) +
    theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = 'none')

title: Lecture 6
text:
Concepts of hypothesis testing: Errors

If you look at the graphs, you’ll see that if you move the observed sample mean to the right, the Type I error area (blue) shrinks, and the Type II error area (red) grows. And vice versa.
Which means that you cannot minimize both types of errors simultaneously.


The trade-off between Type I and Type II errors

Decreasing the probability of one type of error increases the probability of the other type of error. So you have to choose which type of error is more important to minimize in your context.
Generally speaking, Type I errors are considered more serious in scientific contexts, while Type II errors may be more tolerable in exploratory contexts. So we usually set a low significance level (\(\alpha\)) to minimize Type I errors, and find technical ways to reduce Type II errors (like increasing sample size).

title: Lecture 6
text:
Summary

We can use data to make decisions about hypotheses about parameters
We use probability to quantify the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis
We make decisions based on this evidence, but are aware that we might be wrong
We can make two types of errors: Type I (false positive) and Type II (false negative)
There is a trade-off between Type I and Type II errors
We usually set a low significance level (\(\alpha\)) to minimize Type I errors, and find technical ways to reduce Type II errors (like increasing sample size)

title: Lecture 6
text:
Scenario
In the state of South Carolina, there is a concern that young people of working age (20-35) are leaving the state for better opportunities elsewhere. Around 15% of this age group own homes, compared to a national average of 20%. Home-owners have a 1% chance of leaving the state, while renters and non-home-owners have a 15% chance of leaving the state. A new program is being considered to provide incentives for young renters to stay in the state. The program will cost $1000 per person who takes it up, and is expected to reduce the chance of leaving the state from 15% to 10%. It is expected that 30% of renters will take up the program. The average cost of a person leaving the state is estimated to be $50,000 in lost tax revenue and economic activity. We will simulate the impact of this program on a population reflecting the population of South Carolina in 2019, using usdata::pop_age_2019.

section: Agenda and goals for the day

Agenda and goals for the day
