title: Lecture 8
text:
Bootstrapping, revisited

Bootstrapping is resampling your data, recomputing your statistic, and seeing the distribution of the statistic over the resampling
Plenty of theory work in the 90s showed that the bootstrap variance estimate is very close to what you would get if you could generate the sampling distribution

What do I mean by this?

Getting a good estimate of the variability allows us to make good inferences and plan studies

title: Lecture 8
section: Using the bootstrap in machine learning
text:
Using the bootstrap in machine learning
Let’s look at linear regression


Code
library(rsample)
library(broom)
library(tidyverse) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
set.seed(8459)
boots <- bootstraps(iris, times = 1000)
boot_results <- boots |>
  mutate(
      models = map(splits, ~lm(Petal.Length ~Sepal.Length, data = analysis(.x))),
      coef = map(models, tidy)
  ) |>
unnest(coef)

boot_coefs <- boot_results |> select(id, term, estimate) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate) 

ggplot(data = iris, aes(y = Petal.Length, x = Sepal.Length))+
    geom_point() + 
    geom_abline(data = boot_coefs, aes(intercept = `(Intercept)`, slope = Sepal.Length), color = 'gray', alpha = 0.2) + 
    geom_smooth( method = 'lm', color = 'blue')

title: Lecture 8
section: Using bootstrap to look at uncertainty in prediction
text:
Using bootstrap to look at uncertainty in prediction


Code
library(randomForest)
iris <- iris |> rownames_to_column('id')
boots <- bootstraps(iris, times = 50)

# For each split: train RF, predict assessment (OOB) set
oob_pred_tbl <- map_dfr(
  boots$splits,
  function(split) {
    train_data <- analysis(split)
    oob_data <- assessment(split)
    rf_fit <- randomForest(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width + Petal.Length + Petal.Width, data = train_data)
    if (nrow(oob_data) > 0) {
      pred <- predict(rf_fit, newdata = oob_data)
      tibble(
        row_id = oob_data$id,
        oob_pred = pred
      )
    }
  }
)
iris |> full_join(oob_pred_tbl, by = c('id' = 'row_id')) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Petal.Length)) + 
        geom_point(aes(y = Sepal.Length), color = 'gray', alpha = 0.2) + 
        geom_point(aes(y = oob_pred), color = 'black')

title: Lecture 8
section: Frequentists see probability as long-term frequencies
text:
Frequentists see probability as long-term frequencies
The underlying idea in frequentist frameworks is that one can observe a phenomenon repeatedly over time and establish the distribution of the outcome of interest

In reality, we utilize idealized models (Binomial, Normal, etc) to model these “long term” probabilities


The practice is based on the concept of multiple repetitions of the same experiment and what might happen

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
The central limit theorem
This says that, as you take larger and larger samples, the distribution of the sample mean, over repeated identical experiments, will look like a normal distribution



Theorem


Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are independent and identically distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then
\[
\sqrt{n}(\bar{X_n} - \mu)/\sigma \rightarrow^d N(0,1)
\]

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
The weak law of large numbers (WLLN)



Theorem


Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be independent and identically distributed random variables with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Then the sample mean \(\bar{X_n}\) goes in probability to the population mean \(\mu\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\).
\[
\Pr (|\bar{X_n} - \mu | > \epsilon) \rightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n\rightarrow\infty
\]

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)
We postulate a null hypothesis \(H_0\) and an alternative hypothesis \(H_1\). We devise a statistical test \(\phi(X)\) that attempts to judge when the data provides sufficient evidence to favor \(H_1\) over \(H_0\) (which is often a strawman). This test can only reject \(H_0\). The test \(\phi(X)\) takes values 1 (reject \(H_0\)) and 0 (does not reject \(H_0\)).
The test \(\phi(X)\) can incur two kinds of errors:

Type I error: P((X) = 1 | \(H_0\) is true)
Type II error: P((X) = 0 | \(H_0\) is false)


We also will see another quantity, statistical power of a test, which is defined as 1 - Type II error, i.e., P((X) = 1 | \(H_0\) is false)

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)
The Neymann-Pearson paradigm of NHST states that we fix the Type I error at some number \(\alpha\), and proceed to find that optimal test \(\phi(X)\) that maximizes the statistical power, i.e., minimizes the Type II error, usually denoted by \(\beta\).
For simple hypothesis, such a test is generally of the form
\[
\phi (X) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1& T(X) \geq c\\
0 & T(X) < c
\end{array}
\right.
\]
for some test statistic T(X) and some number \(c\), where \(c\) is determined by the value of \(\alpha\).



Example


The one-sample test for the mean, \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) vs \(H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0\) rejects the null hypotheses if
\[
|\sqrt{n}(\bar{X_n} - \mu_0)/s| > z_{1-\alpha/2}
\]

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)
The p-value gives the probability, under \(H_0\) of seeing an observation at least as extreme as the one we observed

Note, this is based on the idea of repeated identical experiments

For most statistical tests, the observed value of the test statistic is compared to quantiles of the (idealized) sampling distribution (often the normal distribution due to the CLT) to get the p-value

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
Confidence intervals
We assume that there is a true value of a parameter \(\theta\).
We specify a number \(0<\alpha<1\) and define a bivariate statistic (L(X), U(X)) so that, over repeated random samples of the same size from the underlying population, the computed interval from L(X) to U(X) will miss the true value of \(\theta\) in \(100\alpha\) % of the samples.






Warning


What is random in a confidence interval is the actual computed interval!!



Confidence intervals are almost always misinterpreted to mean that “there is a 95% chance that the true parameter falls within the interval”, rather than “95% of the time, intervals constructed in this manner will cover the true parameter”

title: Lecture 8
text:
Tools of the trade
Confidence intervals

title: Lecture 8
text:
Pitfalls of the frequentist approach

All arguments are based on non-observable “repeated experiments” rather than solely based on the data at hand
The p-value, which is the basis of much inference, is based on the assumption that \(H_0\) is true, which is unverifiable. It is saying that, if we assume that, how unlikely are we to see what we’re seeing. It also just says that, so we can’t actually infer that the alternative \(H_1\) is more plausible (ever!!) or “correct”, or what kinds of \(H_1\) would have the data at hand be more plausible.
The p-value by itself is not very useful without the domain context, and the corresponding effect size. Recall that the p-value is just an indication of the signal-to-noise ratio in the data, and so with very precise data, even a very small signal can have a small p-value
The need for preserving overall Type I error results in the need for multiple comparisons corrections (essentially reducing the p-value threshold on a per-test basis), but also results in significant loss of power and hence loss of detectable signals
The confidence interval is very frequently mis-interpreted as the chance that the true value of \(\theta\) lies in the interval is \(100(1-\alpha)\)%. As we shall see, this is the interpretation of the Bayesian credible interval

title: Lecture 8
text:
What is Bayesian analysis?

A Bayesian analysis is a particular approach of using probabilities to answer statistical problems

title: Lecture 8
section: What question should we ask our data to inform decision making?
text:
What question should we ask our data to inform decision making?

title: Lecture 8
section: What question should we ask our data to inform decision making?
text:
What question should we ask our data to inform decision making?
It is well-established and convenient to ask this question:




“What is the chance of getting this data if my null hypothesis is true?”  (or “what is the p-value?”)




A Bayesian analysis asks and can answer the question:




“Given the data and everything I already know, what are the chances that my hypothesis is correct?”




There are many advantages to framing the question in a Bayesian way that can help us make faster and more robust decisions

title: Lecture 8
text:
The Bayesian framework

The parameter of interest \(\theta\) is treated as a variable, not a constant.
\(\theta\) is a random variable with a distribution denoted by \(p(\theta)\), called the prior distribution



The data \(D = X_1,\dots,X_n\) comes as i.i.d. data from a data model defined by a probability distribution \(p(D|\theta)\) dependent on \(\theta\).
The p.d.f./p.m.f of this distribution, defined as a function of the data, is called the likelihood \(L(\theta | D)\).



The posterior distribution can be computed as
\[
p(\theta | D) \propto p(\theta) p(D | \theta)
\]



Why do we have the \(\propto\)?

title: Lecture 8
text:
Bayesian inference
Bayesian inference is entirely based on the posterior distribution \(p(\theta | D)\)

We can ask and quantify questions like \(P(\theta \in (-1, 1) | D)\), \(P(\theta > 2| D)\), …
Inference becomes an estimation problem
We can compute credible intervals (CR) from \(P(\theta \in CR | D) = 0.95\)

We can actually quantify the chance that a hypothesis is true.
If \(H_0: \theta \in\Theta_0\) vs \(H_1: \theta \in \Theta_1\) then we can compute
\[
P(\theta \in \Theta_0 | D), \quad P(\theta\in\Theta_1 | D)
\]







No longer a strawman


In NHST (frequentism), the \(H_0\) is set up to be a strawman to negate.
In the Bayesian setup, \(H_0\) can actually be a substantive hypothesis of interest, and we can actually evaluate the likelihood of it being true given the data, or see how much the data we see changes the likelihood of the hypothesis. \(H_1\) is no longer the alternative that we want to get evidence for, but just another hypothesis to contrast with \(H_0\). This is quite a philosophic difference.

title: Lecture 8
text:
CONTROVERSY: The prior distribution
To get to the posterior, one must first define a prior distribution \(p(\theta)\) for the parameters of interest

This has been one of the most controversial parts of the Bayesian method
Critics have said that the specification of the prior makes the process subjective, which can bias our inference

We “should be completely agnostic”, which is what frequentist methods appear to be





We are rarely completely ignorant about values a parameter can take
Domain knowledge often dictates the prior distribution
“Priors are never arbitrary” but can be justified by domain knowledge (Richard McElreath, 2023)
The frequentist method corresponds often to the assumption of a uniform distribution as a prior. This too, is a choice.

title: Lecture 8
text:
The prior distribution
The prior distribution theoretically can be elicited from expert opinion and knowledge as well as prior data. This is a process.

We will often choose prior distributions based on heuristic considerations of the constraints a parameter will be under
There is a choice of priors, called conjugate priors, for a particular data model (likelihood function), so that using those priors results in the posterior being in the same family as the prior

One can get analytic solutions to the posterior

title: Lecture 8
text:
Conjugate priors
If you have a binary (yes/no) variable that you are observing, and you’re interested in the probabilty of a “yes”, taking the prior as a Beta distribution results in a Beta posterior.
\[
\theta \sim Beta(\alpha,\beta)\\
X_1, \dots, X_n \sim Bin(1, \theta)
\] then \[
\theta | X \sim Beta(\alpha + \sum X, \beta + n - \sum X)
\]
The parameters \(\alpha, \beta\) are called hyperparameters.






Hyperparameters can have priors, too

title: Lecture 8
text:
Conjugate priors
If our data comes from a \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) distribution with known \(\sigma\), then
\[
\mu \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)\\
X_1,\dots,X_n \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)
\]
then
\[
\mu | X_1,\dots,X_n
\sim
N\left(\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\sigma_0^2}+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}} \left( \frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{\sum X}{\sigma^2}\right), \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}
\right)
\]






Tip


A list of conjugate priors is given here

title: Lecture 8
section: How much does the prior matter
text:
How much does the prior matter
Suppose we do a coin tossing experiment with a biased coin with P(heads) = 0.7. From a Bayesian approach, we’ll put a prior distribution of Beta(1,1) on it.
Let’s see how the posterior changes as we toss more coins

title: Lecture 8
text:
Prior predictive checks
We want to see if our choice of prior leads to data that is reasonably what we would expect. This is called a prior predictive check, and is achieved by generating data based on the prior choice.

title: Lecture 8
text:
Computing the posterior
With a conjugate prior, computing the posterior distribution is analytic.
Let us consider the beta-binomial conjugate family, with a \(Beta(1,1)\) prior









Play around with how much data is needed to move the ticker on our knowledge of \(p\).

title: Lecture 8
text:
Bayes factor
The Bayes factor is the relative evidence for different models (or different parameter sets under the same model) given the data
\[
k = \frac{P(\Theta_1 | D)}{P(\Theta_2 | D)}
\]
Kass & Raftery (2005) provided a rule of thumb when evaluating Bayes factors

title: Lecture 8
text:
An example
We’re interested in evaluating an assay to see if it is sensitive enough for our purposes. We deem an assay to be acceptable if it has sensitivity of 95% or above. It is considered unacceptable if the sensitivity is below 90%.
We run the test on 100 sick people and get 95 positive tests.
The model
\[
\theta \sim Beta(4,1)\\
X \sim Bin(100, \theta)
\]
Under this conjugate prior, the posterior distribution of \(\theta\) is Beta(4 + X, 1 + 100 - X).

Overview
Learning Objectives:

Understand the fundamentals of predictive modeling

Make informed decisions about model selection and tuning

title: Lecture 12
text:
What is Predictive Modeling?
Definition: Predictive modeling uses statistical and machine learning techniques to predict future outcomes based on historical data.
Key Components:

Training Data: Historical data used to build the model
Features (Predictors): Input variables used for prediction
Target Variable: The outcome we want to predict
Model Algorithm: The mathematical approach (e.g., linear regression, random forest)
Predictions: The model’s outputs for new data

Two Main Types:

Regression: Predicting continuous values (e.g., temperature, species abundance)
Classification: Predicting categories (e.g., species presence/absence, habitat type)

title: Lecture 12
text:
The Fundamental Challenge: Generalization
The Goal: Build a model that performs well on new, unseen data
The Problem: Models can perform well on training data but poorly on new data
Why This Matters:

A model that only works on training data is useless for predictions
We need models that capture true patterns, not random noise
This is the essence of the generalization problem

Example from Environmental Science:

Training on water quality data from 2020
Want to predict water quality in 2025
Model must learn general patterns, not year-specific quirks

title: Lecture 12
text:
Problem #1: Overfitting
What is Overfitting?
Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too well, including random noise and specific details that don’t generalize to new data.
Characteristics:

High performance on training data
Poor performance on test/new data
Model is too complex for the amount of data
Captures noise instead of signal

Real-World Analogy:
Like a student who memorizes specific exam questions instead of understanding concepts—they’ll fail when questions are worded differently.
Symptoms:

Large gap between training and validation accuracy
Model has too many parameters relative to data size
Unstable predictions (small input changes cause large output changes)

title: Lecture 12
text:
Problem #1: Overfitting (Example)
R Example: Polynomial Regression with Tidymodels


Code
library(tidymodels)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

# Generate data with noise
set.seed(42)
x <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.5)
y_true <- 2 * x + 5
y_observed <- y_true + rnorm(length(x), sd = 3)
train_data <- tibble(x = x, y = y_observed)

# Simple linear model (appropriate)
simple_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

simple_fit <- simple_spec %>%
  fit(y ~ x, data = train_data)

# Overfit model (polynomial degree 15)
overfit_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

overfit_fit <- overfit_spec %>%
  fit(y ~ poly(x, 15), data = train_data)

# Generate predictions
x_new <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)
pred_data <- tibble(x = x_new)

pred_data$simple <- predict(simple_fit, pred_data)$.pred
pred_data$overfit <- predict(overfit_fit, pred_data)$.pred

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = train_data, aes(x, y), size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = pred_data, aes(x, simple), color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = pred_data, aes(x, overfit), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Simple (blue) vs Overfit (red) Model")









What You’ll See: The overfit model wiggles through every point but won’t generalize well.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Problem #2: Underfitting
What is Underfitting?
Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the data.
Characteristics:

Poor performance on both training and test data
Model lacks sufficient complexity
Fails to capture important relationships
Too much bias toward simplicity

Real-World Analogy:
Like trying to predict species diversity using only one environmental variable when multiple factors matter.
Symptoms:

Low accuracy on training data
Model predictions are systematically wrong
Clear patterns in residual plots
Important features are ignored

title: Lecture 12
text:
The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
Two Sources of Prediction Error:

Bias: Error from overly simplistic assumptions

High bias → underfitting
Model consistently misses the true pattern

Variance: Error from sensitivity to training data fluctuations

High variance → overfitting
Model changes dramatically with different training samples


The Tradeoff: - Increasing model complexity reduces bias but increases variance - Decreasing complexity reduces variance but increases bias - Goal: Find the sweet spot that minimizes total error
Formula:
Total Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Error

title: Lecture 12
text:
Bias-Variance Tradeoff (Visualization)
R Example with Tidymodels:


Code
library(tidymodels)
library(ggplot2)

# Simulate model complexity vs error
complexity <- seq(1, 20, by = 0.5)
bias <- 10 / complexity + 0.5
variance <- 0.1 * complexity
total_error <- bias + variance

df <- tibble(
  Complexity = rep(complexity, 3),
  Error = c(bias, variance, total_error),
  Type = rep(c("Bias²", "Variance", "Total Error"), each = length(complexity))
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = Complexity, y = Error, color = Type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = complexity[which.min(total_error)],
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Bias-Variance Tradeoff",
    x = "Model Complexity",
    y = "Prediction Error"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)









Key Insight: The optimal model complexity minimizes total error, not bias or variance individually.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #1: Train-Test Split
What is it?
Splitting your data into separate sets for training and evaluation ensures honest assessment of model performance.
The Method:

Training Set (70-80%): Used to fit the model
Test Set (20-30%): Used to evaluate final performance
Test data is never seen during training

Why It Works:

Simulates real-world prediction scenario
Prevents overfitting to the entire dataset
Provides unbiased performance estimate

Important: The split should be random to avoid systematic bias.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #1: Train-Test Split (Example)
R Example with Tidymodels: The iris data


Code
library(tidymodels)

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Load data
data(iris)

# Create stratified 80-20 split
# (stratified ensures balanced classes)
iris_split <- initial_split(
  iris,
  prop = 0.8,
  strata = Species
)

# Extract training and test sets
train_data <- training(iris_split)
test_data <- testing(iris_split)

# Check dimensions and class balance
# cat("Training samples:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
# cat("Test samples:", nrow(test_data), "\n")

# cat("\nTraining class distribution:\n")
# print(table(train_data$Species))

# cat("\nTest class distribution:\n")
# print(table(test_data$Species))

# Define model specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 100) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Fit model on training data
rf_fit <- rf_spec %>%
  fit(Species ~ ., data = train_data)

# Evaluate on test data
test_results <- test_data %>%
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, test_data)) %>%
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, test_data, type = "prob"))

# Confusion matrix
conf_mat(test_results, truth = Species, estimate = .pred_class)


            Truth
Prediction   setosa versicolor virginica
  setosa         10          0         0
  versicolor      0         10         2
  virginica       0          0         8

# Accuracy

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric  .estimator .estimate
  <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
1 accuracy multiclass     0.933


Problem Solved: Prevents overfitting by evaluating on unseen data.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #2: K-Fold Cross-Validation
What is it?
A more robust evaluation method that uses multiple train-test splits to get a better estimate of model performance.
The Method:

Divide data into K equal parts (folds), typically K=5 or K=10
For each fold:

Train on K-1 folds
Test on the remaining fold

Average the performance across all K iterations

Why It’s Better Than Single Split:

More stable performance estimate
Uses all data for both training and testing
Reduces impact of lucky/unlucky splits
Better for smaller datasets

Common Choices:

K=10: Most common, good balance
K=5: Faster, still reliable
Leave-One-Out (LOO): Maximum data use, computationally expensive

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #2: K-Fold Cross-Validation (Example)
R Example with Tidymodels:


Code
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(123)

# Load data
data(iris)

# Create 10-fold cross-validation
iris_folds <- vfold_cv(iris, v = 10, strata = Species)

# Define model specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 100) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Create workflow
rf_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(rf_spec) %>%
  add_formula(Species ~ .)

# Fit resamples
rf_results <- rf_workflow %>%
  fit_resamples(
    resamples = iris_folds,
    metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc),
    control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
  )

# View results
collect_metrics(rf_results)

title: Lecture 12
text:
Evaluation Metrics: Regression
For Continuous Predictions (temperature, biomass, etc.)


1. Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
MAE = mean(|actual - predicted|)

Easy to interpret: average prediction error in original units
Not sensitive to outliers

2. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)²))

Penalizes large errors more than MAE
Same units as target variable
More commonly used than MAE


3. R-squared (R²)
R² = 1 - (SS_residual / SS_total)

Proportion of variance explained by model
Ranges from 0 to 1 (higher is better)
Can be negative for very poor models

When to Use Each:

MAE: When all errors are equally important
RMSE: When large errors are particularly problematic
R²: When comparing models or understanding explained variance

title: Lecture 12
text:
Evaluation Metrics: Regression (Example)
R Example with Tidymodels:




Code
library(tidymodels)
library(MASS) # For Boston dataset

# Load and prepare data
data(Boston)

set.seed(123)

# Split data

title: Lecture 12
text:
Evaluation Metrics: Classification
For Categorical Predictions (species, present/absent, etc.)
The Confusion Matrix:
                  Predicted
                Positive  Negative
Actual Positive    TP        FN
       Negative    FP        TN
Key Metrics:


1. Accuracy: Overall correctness
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) = P(correct predictions)
2. Specificity: Of all actual negatives, how many did we correctly identify?
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) 
            = P(predicted negative | actual negative)
3. Recall (Sensitivity): Of all actual positives, how many did we catch?
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) 
       = P(predicted positive | actual positive)
4. F1-Score: Harmonic mean of precision and recall
F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

5. Precision: When model predicts positive, how often is it correct?
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) 
          = P(actual positive | predicted positive)
          = Positive Predictive Value






Note


Note that Precision is a “forward-looking” metric, while Recall/Sensitivity and Specificity are “backward-looking”, in the sense that we need to know the truth first and then see what we achieved.









Warning


You can have a test/predictive model with very high sensitivity and specificity but low precision if the prevalence of the positive class is very low. This is often used as an example in medical testing to say that a test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity can still have a low positive predictive value (precision) if the disease is rare.
This is also an application of Bayes Rule

title: Lecture 12
section: Classification Metrics: When to Use Each
text:
Classification Metrics: When to Use Each
Accuracy

Use when: Classes are balanced
Problem: Misleading with imbalanced data
Example: 95% accuracy seems good, but if 95% of samples are negative, predicting “always negative” achieves this!

Precision

Use when: False positives are costly
Example: Predicting disease presence—don’t want to unnecessarily alarm patients

Recall

Use when: False negatives are costly
Example: Detecting invasive species—missing one could be disastrous

F1-Score

Use when: Need balance between precision and recall
Example: General classification where both error types matter

Key Insight: Choose metrics based on the cost of errors in your specific context.

title: Lecture 12
section: Advanced Metric: ROC Curve and AUC
text:
Advanced Metric: ROC Curve and AUC
What is ROC?
ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve visualizes classifier performance across all possible decision thresholds.
Components:

X-axis: False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)
Y-axis: True Positive Rate (Recall/Sensitivity)
Each point: Performance at different threshold

AUC (Area Under Curve):

Single number summarizing ROC curve
Ranges from 0.5 (random guessing) to 1.0 (perfect)
Interpretation: Probability that model ranks a random positive instance higher than a random negative instance

Why It’s Useful:

Threshold-independent evaluation
Good for imbalanced datasets
Easy to compare multiple models

title: Lecture 12
text:
ROC Curve and AUC (Example)
R Example with Tidymodels:


Code
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(123)

# Get predicted probabilities
test_results <- test_data %>%
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, test_data, type = "prob"))

# Calculate ROC curve
roc_curve_data <- test_results %>%
  roc_curve(truth = binary, .pred_Adelie, event_level = "first")

# Plot ROC curve
roc_curve_data %>%
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "ROC Curve for Adelie Classification") +
  theme_minimal()









Code
# Calculate AUC
auc_value <- test_results %>%
  roc_auc(truth = binary, .pred_Adelie, event_level = "first")

cat("AUC:", round(auc_value$.estimate, 3), "\n")


AUC: 1 


Code
# Find optimal threshold
# (manually by choosing point closest to top-left corner)
optimal_point <- roc_curve_data %>%
  mutate(distance = sensitivity + specificity - 1) %>%
  slice_max(distance, n = 1)

cat("Optimal threshold:", round(optimal_point$.threshold, 3), "\n")


Optimal threshold: 0.588 


Problem Solved: Evaluate classifier performance independent of threshold choice.

title: Lecture 12

More informative than ROC for imbalanced datasets
Helps choose optimal threshold

AUC-PR:

Area under the Precision-Recall curve
Higher values indicate better performance
Ranges from 0 to 1

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #3: Regularization
What is Regularization?
Regularization adds a penalty to the model’s loss function to discourage overly complex models, helping prevent overfitting.
How It Works:

Original goal: Minimize prediction error
Regularized goal: Minimize prediction error + penalty for complexity

Two Main Types:


1. Ridge Regression (L2 Regularization)
Loss = MSE + λ × Σ(coefficients²)

Shrinks all coefficients toward zero
Never sets coefficients exactly to zero
Good when all features might be relevant


2. Lasso Regression (L1 Regularization)
Loss = MSE + λ × Σ|coefficients|

Can set some coefficients exactly to zero
Performs automatic feature selection
Good when some features are irrelevant


The λ (Penalty) Parameter: Controls strength of regularization (higher = more penalty)

title: Lecture 12
text:
Regularization: Ridge vs Lasso


Ridge Regression (L2):
Advantages:

Handles multicollinearity well
Keeps all features in model
Typically more stable

When to Use:

All features potentially relevant
Features are correlated
Interpretability less important


Lasso Regression (L1):
Advantages:

Automatic feature selection
Produces simpler, more interpretable models
Better for high-dimensional data

When to Use:

Many irrelevant features
Want sparse model
Need interpretability



Elastic Net:

Combines both L1 and L2 (mixture parameter)
Best of both worlds
Extra hyperparameter to tune

title: Lecture 12
text:
Regularization: Ridge Example
R Example with Tidymodels:


Code
library(tidymodels)

# Prepare data
data(mtcars)
set.seed(123)

# Split data
mtcars_split <- initial_split(mtcars, prop = 0.8)
mtcars_train <- training(mtcars_split)
mtcars_test <- testing(mtcars_split)

# Define ridge regression specification (alpha = 0)
ridge_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 0) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

# Create recipe for preprocessing
ridge_recipe <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars_train) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

# Create workflow
ridge_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(ridge_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(ridge_recipe)

# Create grid of penalty values
penalty_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-3, 0)), levels = 50)

# Cross-validation
set.seed(123)
mtcars_folds <- vfold_cv(mtcars_train, v = 5)

# Tune
ridge_tune <- ridge_workflow %>%
  tune_grid(
    resamples = mtcars_folds,
    grid = penalty_grid,
    metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
  )

# Plot results
ridge_tune %>%
  collect_metrics() %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = mean)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Ridge Regression: Cross-Validation",
    x = "Penalty (λ)",
    y = "RMSE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Code

best_penalty <- select_best(ridge_tune, metric = "rmse")
cat("Best penalty:", round(best_penalty$penalty, 4), "\n")


Best penalty: 1

  finalize_workflow(best_penalty) %>%
  fit(mtcars_train)

# Evaluate on test set
test_results <- mtcars_test %>%
  bind_cols(predict(final_ridge, mtcars_test))

test_results %>%
  metrics(truth = mpg, estimate = .pred)

  .metric .estimator .estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #4: Feature Selection
What is Feature Selection?
Choosing a subset of relevant features and removing irrelevant or redundant ones to improve model performance and interpretability.
Why It Matters:

Reduces overfitting (fewer parameters to learn)
Improves model interpretability
Decreases computational cost
Can improve prediction accuracy

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #4: Feature Selection
Three Main Approaches:


1. Filter Methods

Use statistical tests to rank features
Independent of model
Fast but ignores feature interactions
Examples: correlation, variance threshold


2. Wrapper Methods

Use model performance to evaluate subsets
Considers feature interactions
Computationally expensive
Examples: recursive feature elimination


3. Embedded Methods

Feature selection during model training
Balance between filter and wrapper
Examples: Lasso, Random Forest importance

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #5: Ensemble Methods - Bagging
What is Bagging?
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) trains multiple models on different random subsets of data and averages their predictions.
How It Works:

Create K bootstrap samples (sampling with replacement)
Train a model on each sample independently
Aggregate predictions (average for regression, vote for classification)

Why It Works:

Reduces variance without increasing bias
Particularly effective for high-variance models (e.g., decision trees)
Models learn different aspects from different samples

Random Forest:

Most popular bagging method
Bags decision trees
Also randomizes features at each split
Excellent general-purpose algorithm

Key Benefit: Prevents overfitting by averaging out individual model quirks.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #5: Ensemble Methods - Boosting
What is Boosting?
Boosting sequentially trains models, with each new model focusing on correcting errors made by previous models.
How It Works:

Train initial model on all data
Identify misclassified/poorly predicted samples
Train next model with more weight on those difficult samples
Repeat, building sequence of models
Final prediction is weighted combination of all models

Why It Works:

Reduces both bias and variance
Forces models to learn difficult patterns
Each model specializes in different aspects

Popular Algorithms:

AdaBoost: Adjusts sample weights
Gradient Boosting: Fits to residual errors
XGBoost/LightGBM: Optimized implementations

Key Difference from Bagging: Sequential (not parallel) with focus on previous errors.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Boosting Example
R Example with Tidymodels:


Code
library(tidymodels)

# Prepare data for regression
set.seed(123)
data(mtcars)

mtcars_split <- initial_split(mtcars, prop = 0.7)
mtcars_train <- training(mtcars_split)
mtcars_test <- testing(mtcars_split)

# Define XGBoost specification (gradient boosting)
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = 500,
  tree_depth = 3,
  learn_rate = 0.01,
  min_n = 5
) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Create workflow
xgb_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(xgb_spec) %>%
  add_formula(mpg ~ .)

# Fit model
xgb_fit <- xgb_workflow %>%
  fit(mtcars_train)

# Predictions on test set
test_results <- mtcars_test %>%
  bind_cols(predict(xgb_fit, mtcars_test))

# Evaluate
test_metrics <- test_results %>%

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #6: Hyperparameter Tuning
What are Hyperparameters?
Parameters set before training that control the learning process (not learned from data).
Examples:

Number of trees in random forest
Learning rate in gradient boosting
Regularization strength (λ)
Number of neighbors in k-NN
Tree depth, min samples per leaf

Why Tune Them?

Default values rarely optimal
Proper tuning significantly improves performance
Can mean difference between mediocre and excellent model

title: Lecture 12
text:
Solution #6: Hyperparameter Tuning
Two Main Approaches:
1. Grid Search

Tests all combinations of specified values
Exhaustive but thorough
Computationally expensive
Best when parameter space is small

2. Random Search

Tests random combinations
More efficient for large parameter spaces
Often finds good solutions faster
Recommended for initial exploration

title: Lecture 12
section: Putting It All Together: Complete Workflow
text:
Putting It All Together: Complete Workflow
Step-by-Step Predictive Modeling Process:


1. Data Preparation

Clean data, handle missing values
Split into train/test sets
Create cross-validation folds

2. Initial Model Training

Start with simple baseline models
Use cross-validation for evaluation
Check for obvious overfitting/underfitting

3. Feature Engineering

Create relevant features using recipes
Remove irrelevant/redundant features
Use domain knowledge


4. Model Selection

Try multiple algorithms
Compare using consistent metrics
Consider bias-variance tradeoff

5. Hyperparameter Tuning

Use grid, random, or Bayesian search
Optimize on validation/CV folds
Avoid tuning on test set

6. Final Evaluation

Evaluate best model on held-out test set using last_fit()
Report multiple relevant metrics
Check residuals/error patterns

title: Lecture 12
text:
Complete Workflow Example
R Example: Full Tidymodels Pipeline


Code
library(tidymodels)
library(MASS)

set.seed(123)

# Step 1: Data Preparation
data(Boston)

# Initial split
boston_split <- initial_split(Boston, prop = 0.8, strata = medv)
boston_train <- training(boston_split)
boston_test <- testing(boston_split)

# Create CV folds
boston_folds <- vfold_cv(boston_train, v = 5)

# Step 2: Create recipe for preprocessing
boston_recipe <- recipe(medv ~ ., data = boston_train) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.9)

# Step 3: Define multiple model specifications

# Linear regression
lm_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

# Ridge regression
ridge_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 0) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

# Random forest
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# XGBoost
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = 500,
  tree_depth = tune(),
  learn_rate = tune()
) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Step 4: Create workflows
lm_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(lm_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(boston_recipe)

ridge_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(ridge_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(boston_recipe)

rf_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(rf_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(boston_recipe)

xgb_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(xgb_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(boston_recipe)

# Step 5: Evaluate baseline model (linear regression)
lm_results <- lm_workflow %>%
  fit_resamples(
    resamples = boston_folds,
    metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
  )

cat("Linear Regression CV Results:\n")
collect_metrics(lm_results)

# Step 6: Tune more complex models

# Ridge tuning
ridge_results <- ridge_workflow %>%
  tune_grid(
    resamples = boston_folds,
    grid = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-3, 0)), levels = 30),
    metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
  )

# Random Forest tuning
rf_results <- rf_workflow %>%
  tune_grid(
    resamples = boston_folds,
    grid = 10,
    metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
  )

# XGBoost tuning
xgb_results <- xgb_workflow %>%
  tune_grid(
    resamples = boston_folds,
    grid = 10,
    metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
  )

# Step 7: Compare models
cat("\nModel Comparison (CV RMSE):\n")
cat(
  "Linear Regression:",
  round(
    collect_metrics(lm_results) %>%
      filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
      pull(mean),
    3
  ),
  "\n"
)
cat(
  "Ridge Regression:",
  round(show_best(ridge_results, metric = "rmse", n = 1)$mean, 3),
  "\n"
)
cat(
  "Random Forest:",
  round(show_best(rf_results, metric = "rmse", n = 1)$mean, 3),
  "\n"
)
cat(
  "XGBoost:",
  round(show_best(xgb_results, metric = "rmse", n = 1)$mean, 3),
  "\n"
)

# Step 8: Select best model and finalize
best_rf <- select_best(rf_results, metric = "rmse")
final_workflow <- rf_workflow %>%
  finalize_workflow(best_rf)

# Step 9: Final evaluation on test set
final_results <- final_workflow %>%
  last_fit(boston_split)

# Extract test metrics
collect_metrics(final_results)

# Extract test predictions
test_predictions <- collect_predictions(final_results)

# Plot predictions vs actual
test_predictions %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = medv, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Actual", y = "Predicted", title = "Test Set: Predicted vs Actual") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Lecture 12
text:
Calibration
What is Calibration?
Calibration assesses how well predicted probabilities reflect actual outcomes.

Important for classification tasks
A well-calibrated model’s predicted probabilities match observed frequencies

How to Check Calibration:

Calibration plots (predicted vs observed)
Brier score (lower is better)

title: Lecture 12
text:
Calibration Example
R Example with Tidymodels:

Code
library(tidymodels)
library(ggplot2)
library(probably)
set.seed(123)
# Prepare data
# Using Pima Indians diabetes dataset
data("PimaIndiansDiabetes2", package = "mlbench")

diabetes_data <- PimaIndiansDiabetes2 %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  mutate(diabetes = as.factor(ifelse(diabetes == "pos", "pos", "neg")))

# Split data

diabetes_train <- training(diabetes_split)
diabetes_test <- testing(diabetes_split)

# Define logistic regression model

  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Create workflow

# Fit model

# Predictions on test set

  bind_cols(predict(log_reg_fit, diabetes_test, type = "prob")) %>%
  bind_cols(predict(log_reg_fit, diabetes_test))

test_results |>
  cal_plot_breaks(
    truth = diabetes,
    estimate = .pred_pos,
    event_level = 'second'

test_results |>

  )

title: Lecture 12
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid


1. Data Leakage

Problem: Information from test set leaks into training
Example: Normalizing data before splitting
Solution: Always split first, then preprocess (use recipes!)

2. Overfitting to Validation Set

Problem: Tuning hyperparameters repeatedly on same validation set
Solution: Use nested cross-validation or separate validation set

3. Ignoring Class Imbalance

Problem: High accuracy on imbalanced data is misleading
Solution: Use appropriate metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC) and stratified sampling


4. Not Checking Assumptions

Problem: Using linear models on non-linear relationships
Solution: Visualize data, check residuals, consider transformations

5. Test Set Contamination

Problem: Trying many models and reporting best result on test set
Solution: Final test set evaluation should be done exactly once with last_fit()

6. Forgetting to Set Seeds

Problem: Results not reproducible
Solution: Set seed before any random operation

title: Lecture 12
text:
Decision Guide: Which Method When?


Problem: Overfitting

✓ Use cross-validation with fit_resamples()
✓ Apply regularization (Ridge/Lasso with tune())
✓ Feature selection (step_corr(), vip, lasso)
✓ Get more training data
✓ Use ensemble methods (bagging)
✓ Reduce model complexity

Problem: Underfitting

✓ Use more complex model
✓ Add relevant features (recipes)
✓ Reduce regularization penalty
✓ Use ensemble methods (boosting)
✓ Increase trees/iterations


Problem: Limited Data

✓ Use domain knowledge
✓ Use cross-validation (vfold_cv())
✓ Use simpler models
✓ Strong regularization
✓ Feature selection

Problem: High-Dimensional Data

✓ Lasso for feature selection
✓ Random Forest (handles many features)
✓ step_pca() for dimensionality reduction

Problem: Imbalanced Classes

✓ Use precision, recall, F1, AUC
✓ Stratified sampling (strata argument)
✓ step_downsample() or step_upsample()

How much data do I need?

Which algorithm should I start with?

Classification: logistic_reg() → rand_forest() → boost_tree()

title: Brackets in R
text:
There are three kinds of brackets in R

[] are used for extracting elements from arrays, matrices, data frames.

ArraysLists



x[3] is the 3rd element of an array x
d[1,3] is the element in the 1st row and 3rd column of a matrix/data frame d
d[2,] is the entire first row of a matrix/data frame d
d[,4] is the entire 4th column of a matrix/data frame d
d[,'gender'] is the column named gender in a data frame d



To extract single elements, you use a .acidinline[double bracket:] - lst[[3]] is the third element of the list lst - lst[['apple']] is the element named apple in a named list lst
To extract a sub-list, you use .acidinline[single brackets]: + lst[1:3] creates a sub-list with the first 3 elements of lst





() are used for specifying arguments to functions

mean(x) gives the mean of an array of numbers x
summary(d) gives a summary representation of a data frame d
There are several functions used to make the following visualization



Code
ggplot(beaches, aes(x = temperature, y = rainfall)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth() + 
  theme_classic()




{} are used to contain groups of commands/statements


A conditional statement


Code
if (age < 18){
   person <- 'Minor'
} else if (age > 65) {
  person <- 'Senior'
} else {
  person <- 'Adult'
}



A function definition


Code
my_mean <- function(x, na.rm = T){
  if(na.rm){
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  }
  s <- sum(x)
  n <- length(x)
  mn <- s / n # There is a built-in function mean, so I don't use that word
  return(mn)
}

$ medv    <dbl> 24.0, 21.6, 34.7, 33.4, 36.2, 28.7, 22.9, 27.1, 16.5, 18.9, 15…
Almost all the features are numeric, except for chas, which is a binary variable indicating whether the house is adjacent to the Charles River (1 if true, 0 if false).

title: Modeling case study: Boston housing data
text:
EDA


Code
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(BostonHousing, aes(x=medv)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=1, fill='blue', color='black', alpha=0.7) +
  labs(title='Distribution of Median Value of Homes', x='Median Value (in $1000s)', y='Frequency') +
  theme_minimal()









The histogram shows that the distribution of medv is right-skewed, with a few high-value homes pulling the mean up. Most homes are valued between $10,000 and $30,000.














NoteExercise



Change the predictor in the code above and explore bivariate relationships with medv using visualizations


We will see that there are fairly strong correlations of medv with the different predictors, and many of the relations are non-linear.

title: Modeling case study: Boston housing data
text:
Modeling
Even if we eventually want to do and inferential statistical model, when you have many predictors which may or may not have linear relationships with the target (medv), and may have varying degrees of correlation with each other, it is often initially a fruitful exercise to fit a machine learning model that can account for the data complexity before dropping down to an explanatory statistical model. We’ll try using a random forest model.









This notation medv ~ . means include all available predictors in the right hand side







NoteExercise



Play around with the value of nodesize in the code above (it can range from 1 to 506) and see how the prediction quality changes. You’re looking for bias (how poorly the data aligns the the green line which shows where the observed and predicted values would be equal) and variance (how much the predictions are spread out or tight)


You can get a sense of what variables might be important for the prediction by using what are called variable importances (for regression problems like this one, look at the %IncMSE one, which shows the % increase in the RMSE). Note that these will change as you change the nodesize value.








This plot shows that rm and lstat are the most predictive of the predictors, but others have some influence on the predictions






Tip



What the variable importances are showing is how much worse the prediction would be if you replaced each variable with random noise, which would have no relationship with medv. There are other variable importance scores that can be computed.
For a linear regression, the estimated coefficients (or their squared values) work as variable importance scores
